forks.name: device-activity-tracker
forks.description: A phone number can reveal whether a device is active, in standby or offline (and more). This PoC demonstrates how delivery receipts + RTT timing leak sensitive device-activity patterns. (WhatsApp / Signal)
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Organizations that rely on WhatsApp or Signal for confidential communications have no built‑in way to detect whether a target phone is actively being used, idle, or offline. An adversary can infer user behavior simply by measuring the round‑trip time (RTT) of delivery receipts, exposing privacy‑sensitive activity patterns.

What This Does  
The repository implements the proof‑of‑concept described in “Careless Whisper: Exploiting Silent Delivery Receipts to Monitor Users on Mobile Instant Messengers.”  

 Backend logic lives in src/ – src/server.ts starts an Express server, src/tracker.ts handles RTT probing, and src/signal-tracker.ts contains the WhatsApp‑specific probe implementation.  
 The React front‑end in client/src/ (e.g., App.tsx, Dashboard.tsx, ContactCard.tsx) visualises real‑time RTTs, classifies the device state (online 🟢, standby 🟡, offline 🔴), and stores historical measurements.  
Dockerisation (Dockerfile, client/Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml) isolates both services, exposing the UI on CLIENTPORT (default 3000) and the API on BACKENDPORT (default 3001).

How To Use It  
Clone & prepare  
   git clone https://github.com/gommzystudio/device-activity-tracker.git
   cd device-activity-tracker
   cp .env.example .env          # edit .env if you need non‑default ports
Run with Docker (recommended)  
   docker compose up --build     # builds both backend and React client

   Access the UI at http://localhost:3000. The QR‑code flow for WhatsApp authentication is rendered automatically.
Run manually (for development)  
   npm install                     # installs root deps (none for backend)
   cd client && npm install && cd ..
   npm run start:server            # executes src/server.ts via ts-node (see package.json scripts)
   npm run start:client            # runs React dev server (client/src/index.tsx)

   After the backend is listening, open the front‑end, scan the QR code, and enter the target phone number (e.g., 491701234567).

Real‑World Use  
A security‑research team can deploy the container on a dedicated monitoring host, point the UI to a list of test numbers, and collect activity timelines for risk assessments. Example workflow:

Start containers
docker compose up -d

In a browser, navigate to http://localhost:3000
→ Scan QR, add target number
→ Observe live RTT chart; export CSV via the UI (implemented in Dashboard.tsx)

The exported data can feed into SIEM dashboards to flag anomalous device‑state changes.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Missing CI/CD – No .github/workflows or other pipeline files; builds and tests are not gated automatically.  
Low – No lockfile – client/package.json and root package.json lack package-lock.json/pnpm-lock.yaml, making reproducible installs nondeterministic.  
Low – Limited test coverage – Only a single React component test (client/src/App.test.tsx) and setup file exist; core tracker logic (src/tracker.ts, src/signal-tracker.ts) is untested.  
Low – Secrets handling – .env.example hints at required variables (ports, possibly WhatsApp credentials) but the repo does not enforce validation; accidental commit of real secrets would be a risk.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README covers Docker usage but does not list required environment variables beyond ports, nor does it describe the expected format of WhatsApp authentication data.  
Info – License present – MIT license (LICENSE) is included, allowing commercial use with attribution.

The Bottom Line  
The project delivers a functional demonstration of RTT‑based device‑activity tracking for WhatsApp/Signal, with a usable UI and Docker deployment scripts. However, the lack of CI, lockfiles, and comprehensive tests limits confidence for production‑grade deployments. It is suitable for security researchers or proof‑of‑concept pilots, but organizations should harden the build pipeline, add unit/integration tests for the tracking core, and ensure secret management before any operational use.

forks.name: advertools
forks.description: advertools - online marketing productivity and analysis tools
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Online marketers routinely wrestle with URL‑level data wrangling – extracting links, reconciling sitemaps, building keyword lists, and checking robots.txt compliance. These tasks are repetitive, prone to manual error, and do not scale when campaigns grow beyond a handful of domains. The advertools package was created to automate the common‑denominator steps so analysts can focus on interpretation rather than data plumbing.

What This Does  
advertools is a collection of independent, DataFrame‑returning functions that follow the UNIX philosophy “do one thing and do it well.” Key capabilities are embodied in the following modules:
advertools/extract.py – parses HTML, extracts headings, links, and metadata.  
advertools/spider.py – crawls sites respecting robots.txt; useful for bulk link audits.  
advertools/robotstxt.py – fetches and parses robots.txt files to determine crawlable paths.  
advertools/sitemaps.py – downloads and validates XML sitemaps, reporting missing or malformed entries.  
advertools/kwgenerate.py – expands a seed keyword list into long‑tail variations.  
advertools/serpclaude.py – queries the Claude‑powered SERP endpoint for position tracking.  

The package’s entry points live in advertools/cli.py and advertools/clidocs/cli.py, allowing ad‑hoc command‑line use or integration into larger pipelines.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The package is published to PyPI and can be installed with the standard pip command shown in the README:

python3 -m pip install advertools

Dependencies are declared in pyproject.toml and setup.cfg; no lockfile is present, so reproducible builds require pinning versions manually or using a tool such as pip‑compile.

Configuration  
Some functions may require external keys. For example, advertools/serpclaude.py contacts a Claude‑based SERP API; the README notes that a valid API token must be supplied, but the repo does not include a dedicated config file or environment‑variable conventions. Users should set the appropriate secret in their shell or CI environment before invoking those functions.

Running it  
The primary CLI is invoked from the package module:

python3 -m advertools.cli --help

or, for the docs‑generation wrapper:

python3 -m advertools.clidocs.cli --help

Individual functions can be imported and called directly from Python, e.g.:

import advertools as at
links = at.extract.extractlinks("https://example.com")

Real‑World Use  
A typical workflow for a mid‑size SEO audit might look like this:

import advertools as at
import pandas as pd
Crawl the site and collect all outbound links
links = at.spider.crawl("https://example.com", maxpages=500)
Filter links that are blocked by robots.txt
allowed = at.robotstxt.isallowed(links["url"], "https://example.com/robots.txt")
Pull sitemap URLs and verify they exist
sitemapurls = at.sitemaps.fetch("https://example.com/sitemap.xml")
valid = at.sitemaps.validate(sitemapurls)
Expand a seed keyword list for the upcoming campaign
keywords = at.kwgenerate.generate("pay‑per‑click", n=5000)
Combine results for downstream analysis
df = pd.concat([links, keywords], axis=1)

The modular design means each step can be run independently or chained, and the resulting DataFrames feed directly into pandas‑based visualization or machine‑learning pipelines.

Code Health & Issues  
Dependency lockfile missing – pyproject.toml lists runtime dependencies but no requirements.txt or uv.lock is committed, making exact reproduction across environments uncertain. (pyproject.toml)  
Test coverage is strong – 59 test files under tests/ include unit tests for crawl, sitemap, robotstxt, and keyword‑generation logic, with a conftest.py providing shared fixtures. CI is configured via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml) and CodeQL scanning (.github/workflows/codeql.yml).  
No explicit configuration file for API secrets – functions that depend on external services (e.g., serpclaude.py) expect the caller to provide credentials; there is no .env or config template in the repo, which can be a friction point for new contributors.  
Modules are well‑documented – each function has an RST doc in docs/ and the package’s init.py exposes a clean public API, but a few edge‑case error paths (e.g., network time‑outs in robotstxt.py) are not wrapped with custom exceptions, relying on the underlying library’s default behaviour.  

The Bottom Line  
advertools delivers a pragmatic set of utilities for the data‑heavy parts of online marketing—crawling, sitemap validation, robots.txt checks, and keyword expansion—without imposing custom data structures. The codebase is test‑rich and CI‑enabled, yet the absence of a dependency lockfile and a centralized secrets config means teams should adopt a pinning

forks.name: VisionDepth3D
forks.description: Generates 3D from 2D videos in multiple output formats using AI-powered depth mapping.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Creators working with 2D video who want stereoscopic 3D output face a fragmented toolchain: separate depth estimators, stereo conversion utilities, and format-specific exporters that rarely integrate cleanly. VisionDepth3D consolidates AI depth mapping, depth fusion, and multi-format 3D export into a single desktop application.

What This Does

VisionDepth3D is a desktop application that generates 3D video from 2D sources using AI-powered depth estimation. The core pipeline combines depth mapping with custom stereo logic to produce "Hybrid 3D" output. It supports multiple depth models, a depth blender for fusing multiple depth sources, and includes a real-time Live 3D mode and an FPS/upscale enhancer using RIFE and Real-ESRGAN.

The repository is a public release page rather than a source distribution. The README states explicitly: "Current protected application source code is maintained privately and is no longer distributed as public source." What's public is documentation, legal notices, and release/installer downloads. Key files include README.md, UserGuide.md, VisionDepth3DMethod.md (technical methodology), and a legal/ directory with five license and third-party notice files. The assets/ folder contains UI screenshots and the logo.

How To Use It

There is no source code to build or install. The project is distributed as compiled installers through official release channels.
Setup: Download the installer from the GitHub releases page or Itch.io. No build step exists in this repository.
Configuration: The application handles configuration internally; no environment variables or config files are exposed in the public repo.
Running it: After installation, launch the desktop application. The UserGuide.md covers the workflow. The UI tabs visible in assets/ (Depth, DepthBlend, Live3D, 3D, FrameTools) indicate the main functional areas.

No commands available - installer-based distribution only
Download the installer from the releases page and run it

Real-World Use

A VR content creator shooting 2D footage with a standard camera wants stereoscopic output for a headset platform. They run footage through VisionDepth3D's depth estimation stage, refine it with the Depth Blender if they have multiple depth sources, then export in the target format and aspect ratio. The Pro tier ($59.99 one-time) removes export limits like watermarks, resolution caps, and render length restrictions.

Code Health & Issues
High - No source code to review: The repository contains documentation and assets only. Security, correctness, and maintainability of the actual application cannot be assessed. The private source is a black box.
Med - No tests or CI: No test files or CI configuration exist in the repo. For a released desktop application, this is expected given the source is private, but it means there is no public evidence of automated quality gates.
Med - Proprietary license with no-derivatives clause: legal/VisionDepth3DEULA.txt and the README prohibit forking, modification, and redistribution. This is a deliberate business decision, but it rules out community contributions and code-level audit.
Low - Documentation-only repo: The legal/ directory is thorough (five files covering third-party model acknowledgments and license notices), which is good hygiene for a product bundling AI models.

The Bottom Line

VisionDepth3D is a commercial desktop product with a public documentation and distribution page, not an open-source codebase. The tool appears purpose-built for its niche and has a documented 23K+ download history, but the closed-source model means you cannot inspect, extend, or independently verify the implementation. Choose it if you want a turnkey 3D conversion tool with a Pro tier; skip it if you need auditable, modifiable source code.

forks.name: pindrop
forks.description: A native macOS menu bar dictation app using local speech-to-text with WhisperKit
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Mac users who need reliable, offline dictation must either rely on Apple’s built‑in Speech Recognition (limited language support) or use third‑party cloud services that expose audio to external servers. Both options compromise privacy or lack flexibility for developers who want to embed transcription in custom macOS workflows.

What This Does  
Pindrop is a native macOS menu‑bar app that captures microphone audio and runs it through local Whisper models via WhisperKit (see Pindrel/AppCoordinator.swift for the transcription flow).  The app can also fall back to cloud providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter) whose API keys are stored in the macOS Keychain.  

Key components:  

 Pindrop/AppCoordinator.swift – orchestrates UI, hot‑key handling, and starts the selected transcription engine.  
 Pindrop/AppLocalization.swift – loads the 31‑language YAML files under Localization/app/.yml and supplies localized strings to SwiftUI views.  
 Pindrop/AppTestMode.swift – toggles a mock transcription pipeline used by the test suite (PindropTests/).  

The Xcode project (Pindrop.xcodeproj/) uses SwiftPM to fetch WhisperKit, FluidAudio, and Sparkle for auto‑updates. CI is defined in .github/workflows/ci.yml, which runs xcodebuild test on macOS runners.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone the repo and open Pindrop.xcodeproj in Xcode 15+.  
Resolve Swift packages (File → Packages → Resolve Package Versions).  
Build the Pindrop scheme:  

xcodebuild -scheme Pindrop -configuration Release clean build

Configuration  
 Local model selection is persisted in UserDefaults via AppCoordinator.  
 Optional cloud keys are entered through the app’s Settings UI; they are saved in the Keychain (no source‑code files expose them).  
 Localization files are edited directly in Localization/app/.yml; the app reloads them at launch.

Running  
Launch the built app (DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Release/Pindrop.app).  
The menu‑bar icon opens a pop‑over where you can:  

 Choose a transcription engine (WhisperKit, Parakeet, SenseVoice, Apple Speech).  
 Press the global hot‑key (default ⌘⇧D) to start push‑to‑talk.  
 View live transcription and export via the UI buttons (JSON, CSV, plain text).  

For developers, the test target can be executed with:  

xcodebuild test -scheme Pindrop -destination 'platform=macOS,arch=arm64'

Real‑World Use  
A content‑creation team can install Pindrop on each Mac, enable the “copy to clipboard” option, and dictate meeting notes directly into any document. Because transcription runs locally, no audio leaves the machine, satisfying GDPR‑style privacy requirements while still providing speaker diarization and multi‑language support.

Code Health & Issues  

 Low – Missing high‑level README – the repository lacks a top‑level README.md that explains build prerequisites, required macOS version, or contribution workflow.  
 Medium – Limited test coverage – only four test files are present; they focus on UI scaffolding and do not exercise the transcription pipelines or error‑handling paths.  
 Low – Hard‑coded hot‑key strings – hot‑key definitions live in AppCoordinator.swift without a user‑configurable fallback, making customization difficult.  
 Low – No automated linting – CI runs xcodebuild test but does not invoke SwiftLint or similar static analysis, so style inconsistencies may go unnoticed.  
Low – Asset bloat – the Assets.xcassets folder contains >150 SVG icons; while harmless, it inflates the repo size and may slow CI checkout.  

No obvious security red flags: API keys are never committed, and the app uses the Keychain for storage. The CI pipeline is functional, and the Xcode project builds without errors on macOS 14+.

The Bottom Line  
Pindrop delivers a fully offline, macOS‑native dictation experience with a solid SwiftUI codebase and optional cloud fallback. It is ready for power users who need privacy‑preserving transcription, but the project would benefit from a comprehensive README, broader test coverage, and configurable hot‑keys before being adopted in a larger enterprise setting.

forks.name: h3.c
forks.description: MiniMax H3 inference engine for Mac computers
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Generating high‑fidelity video from text prompts on Apple‑silicon Macs currently requires heavyweight frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) that are CPU‑bound or need a separate Python runtime. Teams that want a native, low‑overhead solution for on‑device inference lack a ready‑to‑run C/Metal implementation.

What This Does  
h3.c implements a MiniMax‑H3 inference engine that runs entirely on macOS, using Metal for GPU acceleration and BF16 arithmetic. The core logic lives in h3.c/h3.h and the Metal kernels are in h3metal.m and h3shaders.metal. Model‑loading, tokenizer, VAE, and DiT components are split across files such as h3textencoder.c, h3audiovae.c, h3videoencoder.c, and the GPU‑specific wrappers in h3gpu.h/h3gpu.m. The command‑line interface is provided by main.c and h3cli.c, exposing flags documented in the README (e.g., --info, --profile, --steps, --reuse).

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install system dependencies (FFmpeg must be on $PATH)
brew install ffmpeg   # or use your package manager

Build the binary – the Makefile targets the host code and Metal shaders
make -j8

The Makefile compiles all .c files, the Objective‑C .m wrappers, and links the Metal framework. No external libraries are required beyond the macOS SDK.

Configuration  
Download the MiniMax‑H3 model snapshot from Hugging Face and place it at ./MiniMax-H3.  
Verify FFmpeg/FFprobe are reachable (ffmpeg -version). No additional config files are needed; command‑line flags control all runtime options.

Running it  
Inspect model layout without allocating GPU memory
./h3 --info -d ./MiniMax-H3

Interactive prompt session (default BF16, persistent caches)
./h3 -d ./MiniMax-H3 --width 512 --height 512 --steps 6

For a scripted generation with profiling and preview:
./h3 --profile \
    -d ./MiniMax-H3 \
    -p "A red fox walks through fresh snow in a pine forest." \
    --width 512 --height 512 \
    --frames 22 --steps 20 \
    --layers 45 --reuse 2 \
    --show \
    -o outputs/fox-fast.mp4

All flags are defined in h3cli.c and documented via ./h3 --help.

Real‑World Use  
A media‑production pipeline can embed the binary in a macOS build agent to generate short video clips on‑the‑fly. Example wrapper script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
MODEL=./MiniMax-H3
PROMPT=$1
OUT=outputs/$(date +%s).mp4

./h3 --profile -d "$MODEL" -p "$PROMPT" \
     --width 640 --height 360 --frames 30 --steps 25 \
     --show -o "$OUT"
echo "Video saved to $OUT"

The script can be called from a CI job that runs on Apple‑silicon runners, eliminating Python dependencies.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No CI/CD – No .github/workflows or other CI config; builds and tests must be run manually.  
Low – Limited platform guardrails – Objective‑C .m files (h3gpu.m, h3metal.m) assume Xcode command‑line tools are present; missing checks may cause opaque compiler errors on non‑Apple platforms.  
Low – Sparse runtime validation – CLI parsing in h3cli.c does not appear to validate numeric ranges (e.g., --steps >0), which could lead to undefined behavior if a user supplies an extreme value.  
Low – License present – LICENSE file exists, satisfying basic legal compliance.  
Low – Test coverage – 21 test files under tests/ exercise audio, video, Metal, and tokenizer paths, indicating reasonable unit‑test depth, but no automated test runner is wired in the Makefile.  
Low – Documentation – README covers build and basic usage; however, there is no API reference for the library portion (h3*.c/.h), which limits reuse outside the CLI.

The Bottom Line  
h3.c delivers a functional, native MiniMax‑H3 inference pipeline for Apple‑silicon Macs with Metal acceleration, suitable for teams that need fast, on‑device video generation without Python overhead. The codebase is reasonably organized and tested, but the lack of CI and limited input validation mean additional integration effort is required for production reliability. Ideal for solo developers or small teams comfortable managing macOS build environments.

forks.name: apkleaks
forks.description: Scanning APK file for URIs, endpoints & secrets.
forks.summary:
The Problem
Android application security reviews often require scanning APKs for embedded URIs, endpoints, and hardcoded secrets such as API keys. Manual inspection is time-consuming, and many teams need an automated tool that can disassemble the APK and pattern-match against known credential formats across decompiled smali and assets.

What This Does
APKLeaks is a Python-based CLI tool that disassembles APK files using jadx and scans the output against configurable regex patterns. The core logic lives in apkleaks/cli.py, which serves as the entry point; supporting modules include apkleaks/utils.py and apkleaks/colors.py. Pattern definitions are stored in config/regexes.json and config/notkeyhacks.json, and custom rules can be passed via the -p flag. A Dockerfile exists at the repo root for containerized execution, and build configuration is handled through pyproject.toml, Makefile, and requirements.txt. The tool outputs results as plain text or JSON (--json), with a default random filename if -o is omitted.

How To Use It
Setup: Install from PyPI with pip3 install apkleaks, or from source by cloning the repo and running pip3 install -r requirements.txt. For containerized workflows, docker pull dwisiswant0/apkleaks:latest pulls the prebuilt image.

Configuration: Default search rules are in config/regexes.json. Custom patterns follow the JSON structure demonstrated in the README (e.g., {"Amazon AWS Access Key ID": "AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"}) and are supplied with -p /path/to/custom-rules.json.

Running it: Invoke the CLI with apkleaks -f /path/to/file.apk. From source, use python3 apkleaks.py -f /path/to/file.apk. To pass jadx disassembler arguments, use -a/--args, example: apkleaks -f file.apk -a "--deobf --log-level DEBUG". JSON output: apkleaks -f file.apk -o results.json --json.

Real-World Use
A security engineer integrating mobile scanning into a CI pipeline can run apkleaks -f app-debug.apk -o findings.json --json as a build step. The JSON output is pipeline-friendly, and the -a flag allows tuning jadx decompilation options. Results are reviewed for false positives; if critical secrets (e.g., AWS keys matching the AKIA pattern) are detected, the build can be flagged or blocked.

forks.name: DAAAM
forks.description: Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment (DAAAM), a novel approach to real-time, large-scale, spatio-temporal memory
forks.summary:
The Problem

Robots navigating dynamic environments need to answer spatial-temporal queries about what they observe—"where was the red bag?"—but current mapping systems either store raw sensor data without semantic meaning or run offline with heavy compute. DAAAM addresses this by building 4D dynamic scene graphs in real time, fusing segmentation, tracking, and vision-language grounding so a robot can describe objects, their locations, and their trajectories as it moves.

What This Does

DAAAM is a Python-based pipeline that ingests RGB-D or image sequences, runs SAM segmentation, BotSort tracking, and grounding models to produce semantic region descriptions. These feed into Hydra (MIT-SPARK's hierarchical scene graph framework) to construct a spatio-temporal memory. The architecture is modular: src/daaam/segmentation/, src/daaam/tracking/, and src/daaam/grounding/ handle perception; src/daaam/assignment/ contains the optimization-based frontend for assigning descriptions to objects; src/daaam/scenegraph/ builds the graph structure.

A query layer in src/daaam/querymanager/ exposes two interfaces: dam/ for direct graph queries and mmllm/ for multimodal LLM-based natural language answers. The sceneunderstanding/ module provides tools like getobjectsinradius.py and getagenttrajectoryinformation.py that let an LLM reason over the scene graph. Configuration is YAML-driven via config/pipelineconfig.yaml and Hydra integration in src/daaam/hydra/.

How To Use It

Setup: Install dependencies via pip. The repo has requirements.txt and pyproject.toml; there is also install/install.sh which likely handles system-level dependencies (CUDA, TensorRT). No lockfile is present, so pin versions manually for reproducible builds.

pip install -r requirements.txt
bash install/install.sh

Configuration: Edit config/pipelineconfig.yaml to select models (SAM variants in config/sam2/, FastSAM, EfficientViT) and dataset paths. Prompt templates live in config/prompttemplates/. No environment variables are documented in the README.

Running: The primary entry point is scripts/runpipeline.py. A demo query script is at scripts/demoquery.py. The README does not document exact CLI flags; inspect these scripts to determine required arguments.

python scripts/runpipeline.py --config config/pipelineconfig.yaml

Real-World Use

A warehouse robot with an RGB-D camera runs DAAAM continuously. The pipeline segments shelves and tracked objects, assigns semantic descriptions like "blue toolbox on third shelf," and stores them in a dynamic scene graph. When asked "where did I leave the drill?" the mmllm query service retrieves the object's trajectory from the graph and answers with a location and timestamp.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No tests detected – The repo has zero test files. Core logic in assignment/ and scenegraph/ is mathematically complex (optimization, graph construction) and untested. Expect regressions during modification.
Med – No CI/CD – No .github/ or CI config. Nothing gates merges on build or lint; the project relies on contributor discipline.
Low – No dependency lockfile – pyproject.toml and requirements.txt declare ranges, not pinned versions. Reproducing the exact environment across machines is not guaranteed.
Low – sceneunderstanding/init.py – This file appears misnamed (likely should be init.py). Python will not treat it as a package initializer, which may break imports.
Low – Config sprawl – 20 YAML files across config/ with model-specific settings (sam2.1hierabase_plus.yaml, etc.). No schema validation is evident; a typo in a model name fails at runtime.

The Bottom Line

DAAAM is a serious research codebase from MIT-SPARK with a clean modular design and real benchmark results (NaVQA, SG3D). It is not production-ready: the lack of tests and CI makes it risky to extend, and setup requires manual dependency management. Use it for robotics research or as a reference implementation, not as a drop-in system for deployed robots.

forks.name: vision_pilot
forks.description: Free and fully open-source L2 ADAS stack powered by End-to-End AI technology
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Automotive OEMs and Tier‑1 suppliers need a low‑cost, production‑ready L2 ADAS stack that can run on a single front‑facing camera without relying on high‑definition maps. Existing commercial stacks are closed‑source, expensive, and often require heavyweight sensor suites, making rapid prototyping and safety certification difficult.

What This Does  
VisionPilot/ implements a hybrid end‑to‑end ADAS pipeline that fuses perception models (AutoSpeed, AutoSteer, AutoDrive) with rule‑based safety checks. Core logic lives in the C++ modules under VisionPilot/modules/:

 Perception – modules/models/src/.cpp loads ONNX weights (e.g., autodrivefp32.onnx) via modules/engine/src/onnxengine.cpp.  
 Safety guardian – modules/safetyguardian/fusion/ and modules/safetyguardian/planning/ perform lateral/longitudinal fusion and planning, exposing interfaces in include/fusion/.hpp and include/planning/.hpp.  
 Middleware – ROS 2 bridges are provided in modules/middlewareinterfaces/ros2interface/ for camera (cameraros2interface) and vehicle CAN (vehicleros2interface).  

The top‑level executable is built from VisionPilot/app/visionpilot.cpp and launched as a ROS 2 node (visionpilot), consuming configuration from VisionPilot/config/visionpilotros2.conf.

Simulation support is supplied in Simulation/, notably the CARLA ROS 2 bridge (Simulation/CARLA/ROS2/src/carlabridgebringup/) and SODA.Sim adapters, enabling end‑to‑end testing without hardware.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone the repo (including submodules)
git clone --recursive https://github.com/autowarefoundation/visionpilot.git
cd visionpilot

Build the Docker image (includes ROS2, OpenCV, ONNX Runtime)
cd VisionPilot/docker
./build.sh               # wraps: docker build -f Dockerfile .

The Dockerfile pulls an Ubuntu 22.04 base with ROS humble, installs required system packages, and compiles the C++ code via CMake.  

If you prefer a native build, install ROS 2 Humble, OpenCV 4.x, and ONNX Runtime, then run:
colcon build --packages-select visionpilot
source install/setup.bash

Configuration  
Edit VisionPilot/config/visionpilotros2.conf to match your camera topic, CAN interface, and vehicle parameters. The file already contains placeholders for cameratopic, caninterface, and model paths (e.g., models/weights/autodrivefp32.onnx).  

Running  
From the Docker container:
Start the container (mount the source for live updates)
docker run -it --rm \
  -v $(pwd)/VisionPilot:/workspace/VisionPilot \
  visionpilot:latest \
  /bin/bash -c "source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash && \
                source /workspace/VisionPilot/install/setup.bash && \
                ros2 launch visionpilot visionpilot.launch.py"

If using a native install:

forks.name: cocoindex
forks.description: Incremental engine for long horizon agents 🌟 Star if you like it!
forks.summary:
The Problem  
AI agents typically reason over static snapshots of data, leading to stale context as source code, tickets, or meeting notes change.  Teams need a pipeline that continuously ingests only the Δ (delta) and makes fresh context available without re‑processing the entire dataset.

What This Does  
CocoIndex is an incremental sync engine that monitors source locations (codebases, Slack, PDFs, videos, etc.) and updates a persistent index with only the changed pieces.  The repository contains:
Root Cargo.toml – the Rust build manifest that compiles the core engine and benchmarks (benchmarks/filesummarization/rust/src/main.rs, benchmarks/statestore/main.py).  
Python packaging via pyproject.toml files in each benchmark directory (benchmarks/filesummarization/python/pyproject.toml, benchmarks/statestore/pyproject.toml), indicating the engine is also consumable from Python.  
Connector definitions under docs/src/content/docs/connectors/ – modular adapters for S3, Postgres, Neo4j, Qdrant, and other storage targets.  
Benchmark suites (benchmarks/filesummarization/, benchmarks/entityresolution/, benchmarks/statestore/) that exercise summarization, entity resolution, and state‑store incremental updates.  
GitHub Actions CI (.github/workflows/) that runs tests, type‑checks, and document builds on every push.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The repo provides both a Rust and a Python packaging path.  Typical commands are cargo build (from the root, where Cargo.toml lives) and pip install -e . (or uv pip install -e .) from a Python virtual environment, depending on the target language.  
Environment variables for connector credentials are illustrated by benchmarks/entityresolution/.env.example; copy this file to .env and fill in the required keys (e.g., POSTGRESURL, S3BUCKET).  

Configuration  
Define the data sources and target store in a CocoIndex app definition (see docs/src/content/docs/advancedtopics/customtargetconnector.mdx).  The connector code lives under docs/src/content/docs/connectors/.  
Adjust incremental policies (chunk size, polling interval) via the app’s YAML/TOML config; the framework reads these at start‑up and applies them when scanning paths.  

Running it  
To launch the engine with a simple code‑base watch, invoke the CLI that is built from the root Cargo.toml:  

cocoindex serve --source /path/to/code --target postgres://...
Alternatively, run a benchmark directly:  

cargo run --bench filesummarization  # from the repo root
or
python -m benchmarks.filesummarization.python.runner

Consult docs/src/content/docs/gettingstarted/quickstart.mdx for a step‑by‑step walkthrough that mirrors the above commands.

Real‑World Use  
A midsize engineering organization wants its LLM‑based code‑review agent to always see the latest pull‑request diffs.  By configuring CocoIndex with source = /repo/path and target = postgres (via the Postgres connector in docs/src/content/docs/connectors/postgres.mdx), the engine indexes only new/modified files on each push.  The agent then queries the Postgres vector store for similarity‑based “relevant context” queries, receiving up‑to‑date snippets without re‑indexing the entire repository.

Code Health & Issues  
Tests & CI – four test files are present and GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/fastcheck.yml, .github/workflows/test.yml) run on every push, giving confidence that core paths are covered.  
License & Lockfile – LICENSE and Cargo.lock are present, indicating dependency hygiene for the Rust component.  
Environment‑variable handling – the .env.example files exist but are not automatically generated in the CI pipelines; teams must remember to add the .env to .gitignore to avoid committing secrets.  
Connector coverage – over 30 connector docs exist, yet not all are exercised by the benchmark suites; new connectors may lack end‑to‑end integration tests.  
Documentation density – 111 docs files and 118 markdown files provide extensive guides, but the sheer volume can make it hard to locate the exact configuration knobs for a fresh user.  

Overall, the repo shows a clean SDLC structure (CI, license, lockfile) with a few operational gaps around secret management and connector test coverage.

The Bottom Line  
CocoIndex delivers a pragmatic incremental indexing layer that keeps AI agent context fresh with minimal reprocessing.  Its dual Rust/Python APIs, extensive connector catalog, and active CI make it suitable for teams that already maintain a Python‑centric data pipeline and need reliable, live indexing across codebases or enterprise data stores.  Organizations comfortable managing a few environment variables and who can invest in connector test coverage will gain the most; solo developers or teams without existing Rust tooling may find the initial setup overhead higher than a pure‑Python RAG solution.

forks.name: homepage-lite

forks.summary:
The Problem  
Managing a heterogeneous homelab—services, bookmarks, and basic system metrics—usually requires several disparate tools (Grafana, custom scripts, static HTML). Keeping the UI consistent, the status checks lightweight, and the configuration source‑controlled is a recurring pain point.

What This Does  
homepage-lite delivers a single Go binary that serves a responsive dashboard (see templates/index.html) populated from a config.yaml file (documented in README.md). The server (main.go) reads the YAML, watches it for changes, and pushes updates to the browser via Server‑Sent Events (static/app.js). Themes and icons are loaded from static/themes/*.css and static/iconify.min.js. Asset embedding is handled in embed.go / embeddev.go, allowing the binary to run without external static files in production.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The repository provides a Makefile with a build target that compiles the Go source into a 9 MB binary:

make build          # produces ./homepage-lite

The Docker workflow uses the Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml. Build the image and run it:

docker compose up -d   # pulls the image defined in docker-compose.yml

Configuration  
Create a config.yaml (the README shows the required structure). The file must be mounted into the container at /app/config/ or placed at /etc/homepage-lite/config.yaml for the systemd service (homepage-lite.service). No environment variables are required by default.

Running  
Binary: ./homepage-lite (listens on the port defined in config.yaml, default 8888).  
Docker: http://localhost:8888 after docker compose up.  
Systemd: sudo systemctl start homepage-lite (service file provided).

Real‑World Use  
A home‑lab operator can place config.yaml under version control, update it with new service URLs, and rely on the built‑in file watcher to push live UI updates without restarting the service. Example workflow:

git pull origin main          # get latest config
vim config.yaml               # add a new service
UI automatically refreshes within 30 s

In a larger environment, the container can be orchestrated alongside other services, exposing the dashboard on the internal network for quick status checks.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No test files – Repository lacks test.go files; code paths for YAML parsing and SSE are unverified.  
Low – Limited CI – .github/workflows/build.yml builds the binary but does not run tests or linting.  
Low – Hard‑coded paths – embed_dev.go references static asset directories; switching between embed and dev modes requires manual build flag changes.  
Low – Minimal input validation – main.go unmarshals config.yaml without explicit schema checks; malformed YAML could cause a panic.  
Low – Documentation gaps – No schema definition for config.yaml beyond README examples; users must infer required fields.  

No obvious security secrets are committed, and the Dockerfile uses a multi‑stage build to keep the runtime image small.

The Bottom Line  
homepage-lite offers a lightweight, Go‑native dashboard that is easy to containerize and run on modest hardware. It is well‑suited for solo operators or small teams who need a single pane of glass for service health and bookmarks. The main drawbacks are the absence of automated tests and limited validation of user‑supplied configuration, so additional testing and hardening are advisable before production deployment.

forks.name: term.everything
forks.description: Run any GUI app in the terminal❗
forks.summary:
The Problem

GUI applications require a display server. Running them over SSH, in a VM without a monitor, or on a headless server means either installing a full desktop environment or abandoning the GUI entirely. term.everything eliminates that dependency by replacing the display server with your terminal.

What This Does

term.everything is a Linux CLI program that runs GUI applications inside a terminal. It works by implementing a Wayland compositor from scratch (wayland/ directory, 79 files) that renders windows as ANSI escape codes instead of pixels on a monitor. The termeverything/ package handles terminal I/O, raw mode, keycode conversion, and the main event loop. A small C shim (wayland/mmap.c) handles shared memory.

The project targets both X11 and Wayland host systems. It supports standard terminals via ANSI graphics, and full-resolution rendering if the terminal supports image display (kitty, iTerm2). The compositor implements core Wayland protocols (wayland/protocols/) plus xdg-shell, xdg-decoration, and xwayland-shell extensions.

How To Use It

Setup: The repo includes a Makefile and go.mod. Build with make or go build. The distribute.sh script suggests release packaging. No lockfile is present, so go mod tidy may be needed before building.

Configuration: No config files exist. Options are passed as CLI arguments, parsed in termeverything/ParseArgs.go. The help text lives in termeverything/resources/help.md.

Running it: The entry point is main.go. Per the README, download a beta release or build from source. Run with a command that launches a GUI app:

./termeverything firefox

The README shows examples: warp terminal, Firefox, file managers, and Doom. Terminal resolution limits rendering quality; increase rows/columns for better output. For SSH use, run it on the remote host and connect from any terminal.

Real-World Use

A practical scenario: a developer maintains a remote Linux build server. To run a GUI test suite or inspect a web app without X forwarding, they SSH in and run termeverything firefox. The browser renders as ANSI graphics in their local terminal. With a terminal that supports images (kitty), they get near-native resolution over SSH.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No test files – The entire codebase (131 files) has zero tests. The Wayland protocol handling in wayland/MessageDecoder.go and wayland/SocketListener.go is complex and untested.
Med – No CI/CD – No pipeline in .github/ or elsewhere. No automated build or regression gate.
Low – No dependency lockfile – go.mod without go.sum means builds are not reproducible.
Low – Generated protocol code – wayland/generate/ contains generators; the generated .xml.go files are large and will be hard to maintain by hand if upstream protocols change.
Low – Single-maintainer risk – This is a fork of mmulet/term.everything (8071 stars). The project is ambitious; bus-factor risk is real.

The Bottom Line

This is an impressive technical achievement—a functional Wayland compositor in Go that renders to a terminal. It works for demos and niche remote-GUI use cases, but the lack of tests, CI, and lockfile means it is not production-ready. Use it for experimentation or internal tooling, not for critical infrastructure. If you need GUI apps over SSH, it is worth evaluating; if you need reliability, wait for the roadmap's "Term most things" milestone.

forks.name: tinyworlds
forks.description: A minimal implementation of DeepMind's Genie world model
forks.summary:
The Problem

Most video world models require action labels paired with video frames, which limits them to game or robotics data. DeepMind's Genie architecture removes that constraint by inferring latent actions between frames using no prior action data. TinyWorlds is a minimal, readable implementation of that approach, aimed at engineers who want to understand how Genie works rather than just consume it as a black box.

What This Does

TinyWorlds implements the three-stage Genie pipeline: a videotokenizer.py that compresses frames into discrete tokens via finite scalar quantization (fsq.py), a latentactions.py module that infers actions between frame pairs, and a dynamics.py model that predicts the next frame token given the current frame and latent action. The core sequence modeling lives in models/sttransformer.py (space-time transformer).

The repo is structured for staged training. scripts/trainvideotokenizer.py, scripts/trainlatentactions.py, and scripts/traindynamics.py each handle one stage, with scripts/fulltrain.py orchestrating the whole pipeline. Configuration lives in YAML files under configs/ (e.g., training.yaml, inference.yaml), and utils/ contains distributed training, optimizer, and scheduler helpers. The datasets/ folder handles data loading, with a download script (scripts/downloadassets.py) that pulls datasets and pretrained checkpoints from Hugging Face.

How To Use It

Setup: Clone the repo, install dependencies via pip install -r requirements.txt, and set PYTHONPATH to the repo root. The README documents this explicitly.

Configuration: You need a WANDBAPIKEY environment variable for training. Dataset selection happens via command-line overrides (e.g., --dataset=ZELDA), not a config file. Checkpoints are downloaded separately.

Running it: Train end-to-end with scripts/fulltrain.py, or run inference with scripts/runinference.py after pulling the pretrained sonic checkpoints. The README gives exact commands:

Training
python scripts/downloadassets.py datasets --pattern "zeldaframes.h5"
python scripts/fulltrain.py --config configs/training.yaml -- --dataset=ZELDA

Inference
python scripts/downloadassets.py models --suite-name sonic
python scripts/runinference.py --config configs/inference.yaml -- uselatestcheckpoints=true dataset=SONIC

Real-World Use

This fits a research or education workflow where you need to understand latent-action world modeling before applying it to a custom domain. For example, you could train the video tokenizer on your own dataset, then inspect the learned action space via scripts/visualizebatch.py to see whether the latent actions correspond to meaningful transitions. The modular design lets you swap the dataset in datasets/datasets.py and retrain each stage independently, which is useful for iterating on a single component.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No tests - The repo has zero test files. The three training stages and the transformer are nontrivial; untested code paths are a real risk for anyone modifying the internals.
Med - No CI/CD - No .github/ or CI config exists. There's no automated gate for linting, type checking, or regression testing.
Low - No dependency lockfile - requirements.txt declares dependencies without pinned versions. Reproducibility is not guaranteed across environments.
Low - Environment coupling - The README hardcodes PYTHONPATH="/workspace/tinyworlds", which assumes a specific container path. That will break for local development.

The repo itself is cleanly organized with a clear separation between models, scripts, configs, and utilities. Documentation is thorough for a research codebase, and the license is present.

The Bottom Line

TinyWorlds is a well-structured educational implementation of a genuinely interesting architecture, and the staged training design makes it approachable. The lack of tests and CI means it's not production-ready, and the hardcoded paths suggest it was built for a specific container environment. Use it to understand Genie's mechanics or as a starting point for research; don't treat it as a drop-in library.

forks.name: db-studio
forks.description: The modern pgAdmin alternative that works with every database.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers need a lightweight, cross‑database UI to explore schemas, run ad‑hoc queries and manage data without the overhead of pgAdmin or proprietary tools. Existing solutions are often tied to a single RDBMS, require heavy desktop installations, or lack a programmable API.

What This Does  
db‑studio delivers a browser‑based studio that can connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SQLite, MongoDB and Redis through a single command. The core is split into three packages:

 packages/server – a Hono + Node backend that parses DATABASEURL, builds adapters (src/adapters/), and exposes REST endpoints (src/routes/.routes.ts). Entry points such as src/cmd/args.ts and src/cmd/get-db-url.ts drive the CLI.
 packages/proxy – a Cloudflare Workers proxy (src/index.ts) that enforces rate limits (src/limit.ts) and forwards requests to the server, enabling optional edge deployment.
 packages/shared – TypeScript type definitions and constants used by both server and UI, e.g., src/types/database.types.ts.

The UI lives in the root packages/ui (not listed in the file tree but implied by the React stack) and consumes the server API via TanStack Query. The README’s npx db-studio command runs the bundled server and serves the UI on port 3333.

How To Use It  
Install / Run – No build step required for the published package. The repo itself can be started locally with Bun (present in bun.lock and bunfig.toml):
   # Clone and install dependencies
   git clone https://github.com/husamql3/db-studio.git
   cd db-studio
   bun install   # uses bun.lock for deterministic install

   # Start the development server (uses the server entry point)
   bun run db-studio   # equivalent to npx db-studio

   The script defined in packages/server/src/cmd/args.ts reads flags such as --port, --env, and --database-url.
Configuration – Create a .env file in the project root (or any parent) containing:
   DATABASEURL=postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname

   Alternative variable names can be supplied with --var-name. The server reads this via src/utils/parse-database-url.ts.
Running – The CLI launches the Hono server (packages/server/src/index.ts) and serves the React UI (packages/ui). Access it at http://localhost:3333. Use flags for custom ports or to run in “status‑only” mode:
   npx db-studio --port 4000 --status

Real‑World Use  
A micro‑service team can add a db:studio npm script to their repo, allowing any developer to spin up a UI against the service’s own DATABASE_URL without leaving the codebase. Example workflow:

{
  "scripts": {
    "db:studio": "npx db-studio --env .env.local"
  }
}

Running npm run db:studio opens a UI that can query the service’s MySQL instance, edit rows, and export tables via the /api/export endpoint defined in src/routes/.routes.ts.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile for npm – The repo uses bun.lock but no package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml; CI builds that rely on npm could be non‑reproducible.  
Low – Limited CI coverage – GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/*.yml) run lint, bundle‑size and tests, but there is no explicit security scanning (e.g., Dependabot for npm).  
Medium – Adapter error handling – Some adapters (e.g., src/adapters/redis/redis.adapter.ts) forward raw driver errors without sanitisation; could expose internal details to the UI.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README explains CLI flags, but the UI build process (vite config) is not documented; new contributors may need to infer from packages/ui scripts.  
Low – No explicit license file – A LICENSE file exists, but the SPDX identifier is not referenced in package.json, which can cause ambiguity for downstream packaging.  

Overall, the test suite is extensive (≈50 test files) and CI runs vitest, indicating good functional coverage.

The Bottom Line  
db‑studio provides a solid, multi‑database UI built on modern React and a Hono backend, packaged for quick CLI launch. It is ready for teams that need an on‑the‑fly data explorer without heavyweight desktop tools. Minor gaps remain around reproducible npm builds and comprehensive security scanning, but the codebase is well‑tested and the architecture is clear. Suitable for developers comfortable with Bun/Node and who can manage the small CI improvements.

forks.name: codesight
forks.description: Universal AI context generator. Saves thousands of tokens per conversation in Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, and more.
forks.summary:
Problem  
LLM‑driven code assistants repeatedly parse an entire repository to build context, consuming thousands of tokens before any useful suggestion is generated. For teams that use Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, or Codex this overhead inflates cost and slows feedback loops.

What This Does  
codesight inspects a project in a single npx call and produces a compact, structured representation of the codebase. It extracts AST‑level data for TypeScript (via the wasm plugins in plugins/ast/) and regex‑based detectors for 30+ frameworks across 14 languages. The output includes:

 a wiki knowledge base (.codesight/wiki/) generated from the AST (src/ast/ and plugins/ast/),  
 a blast‑radius map (src/detectors/blast-radius.ts) that isolates the impact of a file,  
 a token‑savings benchmark (src/generators/html-report.ts) that quantifies the reduction, and  
 an optional MCP server (src/mcp-server.ts) exposing 14 “code‑assistant tools” via HTTP.

All of this is bundled into the CLI entry point src/index.ts, which is the script executed by npx codesight.

How To Use It  

Run in any project root – no config, no API keys
npx codesight

Generate a persistent markdown wiki
npx codesight --wiki

Open an interactive HTML report in the default browser
npx codesight --open

Start the MCP server (used by Claude Code / Cursor)
npx codesight --mcp

Show blast‑radius for a specific file
npx codesight --blast src/lib/db.ts

Enable native AST plugins (requires Rust/Go toolchains)
npx codesight --native-ast

The CLI reads package.json (or pyproject.toml for Python fixtures) to discover the project's language stack, then dispatches to the appropriate detector modules under src/detectors/. When the --native-ast flag is present it loads the compiled wasm modules built from the Rust source in plugins/ast/rust/src/lib.rs, the Go plugin in plugins/ast/golang/main.go, and the Python plugin in plugins/ast/python/src/lib.rs.

Real‑World Use  
A development team integrates codesight into their pre‑commit hook (src/plugins/githooks/). The hook runs npx codesight --benchmark and writes the token‑saving report to the CI artifacts. During a code review, a reviewer clicks the blast‑radius link for a changed file; the UI (generated by src/generators/html-report.ts) instantly shows which downstream services could be affected, allowing a focused discussion without pulling the entire repository into the LLM.

Code Health & Issues  

 Severity – High – Native AST plugins depend on external toolchains (Rust cargo, Go go). The repo does not ship pre‑built binaries, so CI must install these compilers; missing toolchain on a CI runner will cause failures. (plugins/ast/Cargo.toml, plugins/ast/golang/go.mod)  
 Severity – Medium – Regex‑based detectors (e.g., src/detectors/graph.ts) lack unit tests for edge‑case syntax, which could produce false positives on newer framework versions.  
 Severity – Low – The README advertises “Zero dependencies”, yet the project includes a full package.json with many dev dependencies; this is not a functional issue but may confuse users expecting a single‑file binary.  
 Severity – Low – License file (LICENSE) and CI workflows (.github/workflows/.yml) are present, but there is no explicit security audit step for the wasm plugins. Adding a cargo audit step would improve supply‑chain hygiene.

Overall, the repository contains 68 test files, a complete GitHub Actions pipeline, and comprehensive documentation (docs/wasm-plugins.md, .codesight/.md). The codebase follows a clear separation: AST extraction, detector logic, and output generators are isolated in src/ast/, src/detectors/, and src/generators/ respectively.

Bottom Line  
codesight delivers a practical token‑reduction layer for LLM‑based code assistants, with solid test coverage and CI support. Teams that rely heavily on prompt‑driven workflows will see measurable cost savings, but they must ensure the CI environment can compile the native AST plugins and accept that non‑TS languages are detected via regex, which may need periodic updates.

The guide walks through five evolution stages - from a basic HTTP monitor to a human-in-the-loop agent that can diagnose and remediate issues across UniFi, Proxmox, NAS, and Plex. The content is a companion to a video tutorial, not a standalone codebase. There is no source code, no workflow JSON exports, and no configuration files. The value is the system prompts and the architectural progression they demonstrate. How To Use It Setup: There is no build step. The guide assumes you already have n8n running and Docker installed. Configuration: You need an OpenAI API key (or compatible LLM), a Telegram account for notifications, and optionally Twingate for secure remote access. The README references YOURSERVERIP as a placeholder throughout - you will replace this with your actual server address. Running it: The core workflow is assembled manually in the n8n UI: Create a workflow with a Manual Trigger node Add an AI Agent node with GPT-4o-mini and Simple Memory Attach an HTTP Request tool named website tool Paste the provided system prompts, starting with Stage 1 and progressing through the stages The README contains the exact system prompts for each stage, which is the primary asset. For example, Stage 1's prompt instructs Terry to check http://YOURSERVERIP:8090/ and verify the response contains

NetworkChuck Coffee

. Real-World Use This is a practical tutorial for homelab operators who want an AI agent to handle routine IT tasks. The staged progression is the key insight: start with a narrow monitoring task, expand to diagnostics, then to remediation with approval gates. The "God-Mode Prompt" section shows how to consolidate all capabilities into a single, more autonomous agent. A concrete scenario: Terry checks a website every 5 minutes via a Schedule Trigger. If it fails, Stage 2 prompts have Terry run diagnostics via SSH or HTTP tools. Stage 3 adds fix actions (e.g., docker restart website) but only after human approval through Telegram. This is a workable pattern for production use, provided you trust the tool permissions you grant the agent. The relevant concerns are: Medium - No test files - There are no workflow exports or test fixtures. You cannot verify the prompts work without manually building the workflow. Medium - No CI/CD pipeline - No automated validation of the documented steps. If n8n changes its node APIs, this guide will silently break. Medium - No LICENSE file - Usage and redistribution rights are unclear despite being a fork of a popular repo. Low - No version pinning - The README references specific n8n features (AI Agent node, Simple Memory) without specifying n8n versions. These features are relatively new and may change. The Bottom Line This is a well-structured tutorial for n8n users who want to build an AI agent for homelab automation. The staged prompt design is genuinely good - it teaches a sane progression from monitoring to autonomous action. It is not a drop-in solution; you must manually build the workflow and adapt the prompts to your environment. If you follow NetworkChuck's video and want the prompts in text form, this is exactly what you need. If you are looking for a ready-to-import n8n workflow, this repo will not satisfy you.

forks.description: 197 bioinformatics & life science skills for Claude Code and AI agents — BixBench 92.0% accuracy. RNA-seq, single-cell, drug discovery, proteomics, and more. Powers OmicsHorizon.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Bio‑informatics teams spend weeks curating command‑line arguments, data‑format quirks, and best‑practice notes for each tool (e.g., STAR, DESeq2, scanpy). When an AI coding assistant lacks that domain knowledge, it generates broken pipelines, forcing developers to intervene manually. The gap is a reusable, structured knowledge base that an agent can read and apply without bespoke fine‑tuning.

What This Does  
SciAgent‑Skills supplies 199 self‑contained markdown skill definitions (e.g., skills/genomics-bioinformatics/rnaseq/deseq2-differential-expression/SKILL.md). Each file includes:

 a concise description,  
 runnable code snippets,  
 parameter tables, and  
 troubleshooting tips.  

The repository also ships a Claude‑compatible plugin manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json) and a registry (registry.yaml) that map skill names to their locations. The small Python helper suite (scripts/validateregistry.py, scripts/blindknowledgetest.py) validates that the registry is syntactically correct and that the benchmark data (blindtestresults.csv) matches expectations.

How To Use It  
Create a Python environment – the project uses Pixi (see pixi.toml / pixi.lock).  
   pixi install          # resolves the conda/pip dependencies
   pixi run python -m pip install -e .   # editable install (no package, but registers scripts)
Validate the skill registry – run the supplied script to ensure all SKILL.md files are reachable.  
   pixi run python scripts/validateregistry.py
Add the plugin to Claude Code – copy the .claude-plugin directory into the Claude plugin path or reference it via the marketplace URL contained in marketplace.json. The plugin JSON points to the registry.yaml file, which the agent reads at runtime.
Invoke a skill – within Claude Code, request a task such as “run DESeq2 differential expression”. The agent will locate the matching entry in registry.yaml, retrieve the code block from skills/genomics-bioinformatics/rnaseq/deseq2-differential-expression/SKILL.md, and execute it in the current environment.
Run the benchmark (optional) – to reproduce the reported BixBench score:  
   pixi run python scripts/blindknowledgetest.py blindtestresults.csv

All CI steps are defined in .github/workflows/validate.yml, which runs the validation script and the test suite on each push.

Real‑World Use  
A research group automates an RNA‑seq analysis pipeline. After installing the skill set, a data‑science engineer writes a short prompt to Claude Code:

“Using the DESeq2 skill, compare condition A vs B in counts.tsv and output a volcano plot as volcano.png.”

Claude Code retrieves the snippet from SKILL.md, substitutes the file path, runs the R code via the system R interpreter, and returns the plot. The entire step is reproducible without hand‑typing any R commands, reducing analyst time from hours to minutes.

Code Health & Issues  

 Tests – Medium – 9 test files exist, but they only cover the validation scripts; the markdown skills themselves have no automated verification.  
 Dependency Hygiene – Low – Pixi manages Python packages, yet no explicit lock for external tools (e.g., R, Java) that many skills require, which could cause runtime failures on fresh systems.  
 Documentation – Low – The README explains the concept and benchmark but lacks a quick‑start guide; users must infer commands from pixi.toml and scripts.  
 License – Low – The repository includes LICENSE (CC‑BY‑4.0), satisfying legal reuse, but no SPDX header in source files.  
CI Coverage – Low – The GitHub Actions workflow validates the registry but does not lint markdown or test code snippets, leaving syntax errors undetected.  

Overall, the codebase shows no structural red flags; the layout is clear, and CI runs successfully on push.

The Bottom Line  
SciAgent‑Skills delivers a well‑organized, markdown‑based knowledge base that materially improves AI coding agents on bio‑informatics tasks (92 % BixBench accuracy). It is ready for teams that already use Claude Code or a similar markdown‑aware agent and can tolerate the manual step of installing external toolchains (R, Java, etc.). The primary gaps are limited automated testing of the skill snippets and sparse start‑up documentation; addressing these would make adoption smoother for solo developers.

Technical Briefing: Inventory (RFID Asset Management)

The Problem
Inventory is a React Native mobile application for RFID asset management targeting home and business environments. It tracks item availability via RFID UHF readers, preventing loss and enabling location tracking. The codebase contains 200 files across mobile app, data layer, and native modules, but lacks fundamental SDLC safeguards.

What This Does
The repository split into three logical layers: App/ contains the React Native mobile interface (188 files) with TypeScript components spanning UI elements (Button, Switch, TableView, DatePicker), state hooks (useConfig, useData, useSave), and data processing (getImageDatum, processAssets). Native Android modules in App/android/ handle UART/Bluetooth RFID communication via RFIDWithUHFBLEModule.java and RFIDWithUHFUARTModule.java, while a Rails/Express backend presumably services API endpoints. Shared data logic resides in App/app/data/ defining schemas, types, and hooks—schema.ts, types.ts, and relations.ts appear to govern the data model. Storybook configuration lives in App/.storybook/ for component documentation, and CI pipelines exist under .github/workflows/ for build, lint, and PR greetings.

Running it: The entry point is App/app/App.tsx (the root React Native component). Building the Android app requires App/gradlew assembleRelease or App/gradlew installDebug from the project root. iOS builds would need a Mac environment with CocoaPods installed; no iOS-specific build scripts are visible in the .github/workflows/ directory.

Real-World Use
A warehouse manager equips assets with RFID tags and uses the Inventory mobile app to scan items into/out of inventory. The app communicates with a compatible UHF reader (supported models listed in the docs at docs.inventory.ztg.app) via the native modules. forks.name: claude_code_agent_farm
forks.description: Orchestration framework for running 20+ Claude Code agents in parallel: automated bug fixing, best-practices sweeps, lock-based coordination, and real-time tmux monitoring
forks.summary:
The Problem

Coordinating multiple AI coding agents on a single codebase typically devolves into chaos: agents overwrite each other's changes, run out of context mid-task, and require constant manual supervision. Running agents sequentially is slow, but running them in parallel without coordination is unsafe.

What This Does

claudecodeagentfarm is a Python orchestration framework that runs 20–50 Claude Code sessions in parallel against a target repository. The core logic lives in claudecodeagentfarm.py (the only Python file), which handles agent lifecycle, lock-based coordination to prevent file conflicts, and automatic context clearing when agents approach token limits.

The repo is organized around 34 technology stacks. Each stack has a configs/*.json file (e.g., configs/nextjsconfig.json), a matching prompt template in prompts/ (e.g., prompts/defaultbestpracticespromptnextjs.txt), and a setup script in toolsetupscripts/ (e.g., toolsetupscripts/setupnextjs.sh). The bestpracticesguides/ directory contains 37 stack-specific Markdown guides that agents reference during best-practices sweeps. A viewagents.sh script provides tmux-based real-time monitoring.

How To Use It

Setup — The pyproject.toml declares a Python 3.13+ project managed by uv. Run:

git clone https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claudecodeagentfarm.git
cd claudecodeagentfarm
chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh

Setup configures the required cc alias (ENABLEBACKGROUNDTASKS=1 claude --dangerously-skip-permissions), installs dependencies, and sets up direnv.

Configuration — Each stack's JSON config in configs/ controls agent count, prompts, and behavior. The system requires Claude Code installed and authenticated, plus tmux and git. Project-specific tools (e.g., bun for Next.js) must be pre-installed.

Running — Verify with claude-code-agent-farm doctor --path /path/to/project, then invoke the farm against a target repo. The README documents workflows for bug fixing and best-practices sweeps, but the exact invocation command is not shown in the excerpt — you'll need to check the README's full usage section or run the CLI with --help. Monitoring happens through viewagents.sh.

Real-World Use

A team maintaining a Next.js codebase with known lint violations and deprecated API usage could run a best-practices sweep: the farm spawns N agents, each assigned a chunk of the codebase, all guided by prompts/defaultbestpracticespromptnextjs.txt and constrained by configs/nextjsconfig.json. Lock files prevent two agents from editing the same file. Each agent commits its changes with rich diff summaries, producing an HTML run report for review.

Code Health & Issues
Med — No CI/CD: No .github/ or CI configuration exists. The only test evidence is 4 test files, but with a single Python file and 35 shell scripts, coverage is likely thin. No automated gate prevents regressions.
Low — No dependency lockfile: pyproject.toml declares dependencies without a lockfile, so builds are not reproducible across environments.
Low — Safety-critical alias: The required cc alias uses --dangerously-skip-permissions, meaning agents run with full system access. The setup script patches mis-quoted aliases, which suggests this has been a real failure point.
Low — Shell script sprawl: 35 setup scripts share toolsetupscripts/commonutils.sh, but there's no evidence of shared error handling or idempotency guarantees across all of them.

The Bottom Line

This is a serious, well-structured orchestration tool for teams already invested in Claude Code and willing to accept the operational complexity of parallel AI agents. The 34-stack coverage is genuinely broad, and the lock-based coordination addresses the core safety problem. It's not for solo developers or casual experimentation — the setup surface (tmux, uv, direnv, per-stack toolchains) is substantial, and the --dangerously-skip-permissions requirement demands a controlled environment. For a team running regular AI-assisted maintenance across multiple stacks, it could meaningfully reduce manual review time.

uvx google-agents-cli setup          # installs the CLI and registers the skill packs

Running  
Create a new agent project (Python ADK scaffold)

Generate evaluation traces

Grade the traces

Deploy to Cloud Run (or GKE) using the built Terraform stack
agents-cli deploy --target cloud-run

Each sub‑command maps directly to a module in src/google/agents/cli/ (e.g., eval/, deploy/).

A data‑science team can automate model iteration:

agents-cli scaffold sentiment‑bot --template python
Run the agent against a curated test set

Grade with LLM‑as‑judge and export metrics

Push the best‑scoring version to production
agents-cli deploy --target cloud-run --region us-central1

The workflow is fully reproducible; all Terraform files under basetemplates/shared/deployment/terraform/ provision the required Cloud Run service, IAM bindings, and logging sinks.

forks.name: packet
forks.description: Quick Share client for Linux
forks.summary:
The Problem

Android's Quick Share is the default way to move files between Android devices and other platforms, but Linux has no first-party client. Existing options are either proprietary, incomplete, or require significant setup. Packet addresses this gap by providing a native Linux client for the Quick Share protocol, letting users exchange files with Android devices over Wi-Fi.

What This Does

Packet is a Rust/GTK application that implements a partial version of Google's Quick Share protocol. The core logic lives in src/, with src/main.rs as the entry point and src/objects/ handling both sendtransfer.rs and receivetransfer.rs state machines. The UI is built with GTK's blueprint format (data/resources/ui/window.blp), and the project uses the Meson build system (meson.build) with a Rust backend via Cargo.toml.

The Problem  
ML agents frequently need to reuse low‑level capabilities (e.g., “open a fridge”, “measure a temperature”) but each project rebuilds these skills from scratch. This duplication wastes engineering effort and makes it hard to assess safety or cost of a skill before deployment.

What This Does  
SkillNet supplies an open‑source “skill marketplace” and a lightweight SDK for discovering, installing, authoring, evaluating, and composing those skills. The repository is organized around two main entry points:

 examples/ – runnable notebooks and scripts (createexample.py, evaluateexample.py, searchdemo.py) that demonstrate the SDK workflow.  
 experiments/src/skills/ – a library of concrete skill definitions (e.g., alfworld/alfworld-clean-object/SKILL.md, scienceworld/scienceworld-circuit-builder/SKILL.md). Each skill folder contains a SKILL.md manifest and optional reference documents that the SDK can parse.

The top‑level README.md shows the public API (SkillNetClient) and CLI (skillnet search …, skillnet download …). The package is published on PyPI as skillnet-ai, but the source code for that SDK is not bundled in this fork; it is pulled in via pip install skillnet-ai.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install the published SDK
pip install skillnet-ai   # requires Python 3.10+

Install the experiment‑specific dependencies (optional, for running the demos)
pip install -r experiments/requirements.txt

The requirements.txt lists openai, anthropic, tiktoken, etc., and is the only declared dependency source.

Configuration  
No API key is needed for public search or GitHub downloads. For evaluation/orchestration, the SDK expects the standard OpenAI‑compatible environment variables (APIKEY, BASEURL, SKILLNETMODEL). These are referenced in the README but not hard‑coded anywhere in the repo.

Running It  
Search and download a skill – via the SDK (shown in README.md):

from skillnetai import SkillNetClient

client = SkillNetClient()
results = client.search("pdf understanding", limit=5)
client.download(results[0].skillurl, targetdir="./myskills")

Run the provided demos – e.g., create a skill from a trace:

python examples/createexample.py

Evaluate a skill – e.g.:

python examples/evaluateexample.py

Explore the interactive notebooks – examples/skillnetusagedemo.ipynb and examples/scientificworkflowdemo.ipynb illustrate end‑to‑end pipelines.

If you need to run the AlfWorld or ScienceWorld experiments, invoke the scripts in experiments/:

python experiments/alfworldrun.py   # AlfWorld demo
python experiments/scienceworldrun.py   # ScienceWorld demo

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science platform can embed SkillNet to let analysts pull “CSV summarizer” or “PDF extractor” skills from the public library, evaluate them against internal safety policies, and compose them into a workflow. The platform would:
Call SkillNetClient.search() for needed capabilities.  
Use client.download() to fetch the skill package into a sandboxed execution environment.  
Run client.evaluate(skillpath) to obtain a safety/completeness score.  
Dynamically generate a prompt that strings together the selected skills for a downstream LLM orchestrator.

No obvious security secrets are committed; the repository respects the MIT license.

The Bottom Line  
SkillNet offers a concrete, community‑driven catalogue of reusable agent skills together with a thin Python SDK that can be integrated into larger LLM‑orchestrated systems. The demos and skill library are well‑structured, but the lack of an in‑repo SDK, CI pipeline, and dependency lockfile make it less suitable for production‑grade deployment without additional engineering effort. forks.name: ccglass
forks.description: See what your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Kimi) sends to the model — local proxy + web dashboard
forks.summary:
The Problem

Coding agents like Claude Code and Codex send large, opaque payloads to model APIs. Debugging what actually gets sent — system prompts, tool schemas, message history, token usage — is painful because these CLIs ignore HTTPPROXY/HTTPSPROXY and often use TLS pinning, so standard proxy tools (Charles, mitmproxy) never see the traffic. ccglass solves this by intercepting only the plain HTTP hop to localhost.

What This Does

ccglass is a local reverse-proxy + web dashboard. It sets the client's base-URL env var (e.g. ANTHROPICBASEURL, OPENAIBASEURL) to point at a local proxy (src/forward-proxy.js), which forwards to the real API over HTTPS. The client does its own TLS to localhost, so no CA certs or TLS-pinning bypasses are needed. The dashboard (web/app.js, web/index.html) shows live requests, token/cache/cost, message history with tool calls, agent-loop flow, and turn-to-turn diffs (src/diff.js).

The repo supports 15+ providers via src/providers.js and format parsers in src/formats/ (anthropic.js, openai.js, reasonix.js). It also includes session stats (src/session-stats.js), export (src/export.js), and content-addressed storage (src/ca.js, src/blobs.js) per design docs in docs/superpowers/.

How To Use It

Setup: Install globally via npm (per README): npm install -g ccglass. The package.json confirms npm as the package manager.

Configuration: No config file required. Env vars are set automatically by the tool per provider. For Codex, API-key mode is required (OPENAIAPIKEY); ChatGPT-login mode uses WebSocket and won't be captured. Kimi runs through Claude Code against Moonshot's Anthropic-compatible endpoint.

Running it: The entry point is bin/ccglass.js, which delegates to src/cli.js. Run with no arguments to pick a client interactively, or name one directly:

ccglass claude
ccglass codex
ccglass deepseek

This starts the proxy, launches the client, and opens the dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:57633 (port varies).

Real-World Use

A developer debugging why Claude Code is sending a bloated system prompt or unexpected tool calls to a model. Run ccglass claude, reproduce the issue in the agent, then inspect the dashboard's request view and turn-to-turn diff to see exactly what changed between iterations. This also works for cost tracking — the dashboard buckets by model and session (docs/cost-and-model-bucketing.md), useful for auditing spend across a team's agent usage.

Code Health & Issues
Med — WebSocket gap: Codex in ChatGPT-login mode bypasses OPENAIBASEURL entirely (documented in README). The dashboard will silently show nothing. This is a known limitation, not a bug, but worth flagging.
Med — src/forward-proxy.js handles plain HTTP only. Any client that insists on HTTPS to localhost will fail. The README says this is intentional, but it narrows compatibility.
Low — 25 test files exist covering most modules, but web-live.test.js suggests some tests depend on a running server, which could be flaky in CI. No obvious missing test coverage for src/export.js or src/mcp.js.
Low — No secrets or config files in the repo. CI is present (.github/workflows/ includes publish.yml). License is present. Dependency hygiene looks reasonable given the lockfile.

The Bottom Line

ccglass is a well-scoped, genuinely useful debugging tool for anyone working deeply with coding agents. The architecture is sound — intercepting plain HTTP to localhost avoids the TLS-pinning problem entirely. The main limitation is provider-specific transport quirks (Codex's WebSocket mode), which are documented rather than hidden. Recommended for agent developers, LLM ops engineers, and teams auditing model spend.

 Base URL – defaults to https://api.massive.com; you can override with baseurl= when constructing the client if you still need the legacy api.polygon.io.

from massive import RESTClient

docker build -t massive-demo examples/tools/docker

A data‑engineering pipeline can pull daily aggregates for a watchlist and store them in a data lake:

from massive import RESTClient

watchlist = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "TSLA"]

massive delivers a straightforward, well‑documented Python wrapper for Massive’s market data APIs, handling pagination and base‑URL changes out of the box. The Problem
