What This Does  
llm-council implements a lightweight web UI that orchestrates a “council” of LLMs via the OpenRouter gateway. The backend (backend/main.py) runs a FastAPI server that:
Sends the user prompt to every model listed in backend/config.py (Stage 1).  
Feeds each model the other models’ responses for anonymous ranking (Stage 2).  
Passes the ranked set to a designated chairman model for a consolidated answer (Stage 3).

The frontend (frontend/src/App.jsx and supporting components under frontend/src/components/) displays each stage in separate tabs, letting users inspect raw replies, review rankings, and view the final synthesized response.

Key files:
backend/council.py – core orchestration logic, async calls to OpenRouter via httpx.  
backend/openrouter.py – thin wrapper around the OpenRouter HTTP API.  
frontend/src/api.js – React‑side helper that calls /api/query on the FastAPI server.  

How To Use It  
Install Python dependencies with uv (requires uv >= 0.4)
uv sync                     # reads pyproject.toml, creates .venv
Install frontend dependencies
cd frontend
npm install                 # uses package.json
cd ..
Provide OpenRouter credentials
echo "OPENROUTERAPIKEY=sk-or-…" > .env
(Optional) Adjust the council composition
Edit backend/config.py → COUNCILMODELS / CHAIRMANMODEL
Start both services (the repo supplies a convenience script)
./start.sh                 # runs backend with uv and frontend with npm run dev

If start.sh is unavailable or you prefer manual control:

Backend (FastAPI) on default port 8000
uv run python -m backend.main

Frontend (Vite dev server) on port 5173
cd frontend
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173 in a browser to interact with the council UI.

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can embed this tool in a research notebook to benchmark new prompts across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers. After a single click, the UI returns per‑model answers, peer‑review rankings, and a final aggregated response, reducing the manual copy‑paste cycle and providing a reproducible audit trail stored in data/conversations/ (JSON files).

Example: programmatically fetch the final answer for downstream processing
import requests, json
resp = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:8000/api/query",
    json={"prompt": "Explain transformer attention in 2 sentences"}
)

Overall code organization is clear, with separation between API wrapper, council orchestration, and React UI. Lint configuration (frontend/eslint.config.js) exists, but no corresponding Python linting (e.g., flake8) is present.

llm-council delivers a functional prototype for multi‑LLM comparison with a simple FastAPI + React stack, suitable for quick experiments or internal demos. forks.name: GEA
forks.description: Group Evolving Agents: Open-Ended Self-Improvement via Experience Sharing
forks.summary:
The Problem

Software agents that write code typically operate in isolation. Each agent starts from the same base prompt, attempts a task, and either succeeds or fails without learning from other agents' attempts. This wastes successful strategies and repeats known failures. GEA addresses this by treating a group of agents as a single evolutionary unit, allowing them to share experiences and improve collectively over time.

What This Does

GEA is a research framework for open-ended self-improvement of coding agents. The core loop is implemented in GEAouter.py, the entry point, which orchestrates a group of agents working on SWE-bench tasks. Each agent attempts to fix real GitHub issues from Django and Sphinx, producing patches stored under initial/predictions/. The codingagent.py file defines the base agent behavior—how it reads a task, generates a patch, and writes results.

The system evaluates each patch against the target repository's test suite, with results logged in initial/logs/runevaluation/. Successful patches and their associated reasoning are then shared back into the group's collective experience, which subsequent agents use to inform their own attempts. This experience-sharing mechanism is the key differentiator from single-agent self-improvement approaches. The project builds on the Darwin Gödel Machine and uses SWE-bench and Polyglot benchmarks for evaluation.

How To Use It

Setup: Requires Python 3, Docker, and API keys for OpenAI and Anthropic. The README documents a standard venv + pip install -r requirements.txt flow. Docker must be functional (docker run hello-world). The SWE-bench dependency is cloned and installed separately.

Configuration: Set OPENAIAPIKEY and ANTHROPICAPIKEY as environment variables in ~/.bashrc.

Running: Execute python GEAouter.py from the repo root.

export OPENAIAPIKEY='...'
export ANTHROPICAPIKEY='...'
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd swebench && git clone https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench.git && cd SWE-bench && git checkout dc4c087c2b9e4cefebf2e3d201d27e36 && pip install -e . && cd ../../
python GEAouter.py

Real-World Use

This is a research tool, not a production service. A practical use case: an ML research team studying multi-agent coordination and self-improvement. They would run GEA on a subset of SWE-bench tasks, inspect the generated patches under initial/predictions/ to see how well agents solve real bugs, and analyze the experience-sharing dynamics to understand when group collaboration helps versus when it adds overhead. The analysis/ scripts support plotting and quantitative evaluation of these runs.

Code Health & Issues
Medium - No CI/CD pipeline: No .github/ or CI config exists. The 42 test files are evaluation scripts for SWE-bench tasks, not unit tests for the GEA framework itself. Changes to GEAouter.py or codingagent.py have no automated gate.
Medium - Heavy Docker coupling: The entire evaluation pipeline runs inside Docker containers per task. This makes the system resource-intensive (one container per bug) and fragile if Docker is unavailable or misconfigured in a deployment environment.
Low - Repository hygiene: The repo contains 191 files of evaluation logs and predictions under initial/, which inflates the repo size and mixes generated artifacts with source code. These should be gitignored or stored separately.
Low - Research-stage maturity: The paper is on arXiv and the codebase is built on a prior research project (DGM). Expect rough edges in error handling and configuration, and no production hardening.

The Bottom Line

GEA is a legitimate research contribution to multi-agent self-improvement, with a clear architecture and reproducible evaluation pipeline. It is not production software—no CI, no unit tests, heavy Docker use, and research-grade code quality. Use it if you are studying agent coordination or open-ended self-improvement; skip it if you need a maintainable agent framework for real workloads.

forks.summary:
The Problem

AI agents accumulate skills over time, but most agent frameworks treat skills as static files. There is no unified way to discover which skill applies to a new task, verify which skills actually work in production, or improve skills based on real outcomes. Teams running multiple agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) end up duplicating capabilities and repeating failures across tools.

What This Does

OpenSpace is a skill management layer that sits between your agents and their skills. It provides retrieval (finding the right skill), evaluation (tracking real-world outcomes), sharing (across agents and team members), and evolution (improving skills with each run). The repository contains two applications: apps/dashboard — a React/Vite/TypeScript web dashboard with pages for skills, workflows, agent traces, and skill evolution — and apps/tui — a terminal UI built with Ink that provides a REPL, agent event feeds, permission dialogs, and a vim-mode keybinding system.

The dashboard handles the management view: src/pages/SkillsPage.tsx lists skills, src/pages/SkillDetailPage.tsx shows version history and diffs via src/components/skill-detail/DiffViewer.tsx, and src/pages/EvolutionPage.tsx tracks skill changes over time. The TUI handles the interactive agent experience, with a bridge protocol in apps/tui/src/bridge/protocol.ts that defines structured I/O between the UI and backend agents, plus permission handling in apps/tui/src/hooks/toolPermission/ for interactive tool-use approval.

How To Use It

The repo is a frontend monorepo — there is no backend server, no Python code (despite the README's Python badge), and no pyproject.toml or Dockerfile present. The two package.json files define the apps.

Setup:
cd apps/dashboard
npm install
npm run dev

Configuration: The dashboard requires a .env file based on apps/dashboard/.env.example. The TUI has no .env.example — configuration appears to be handled through user keybinding files loaded by apps/tui/src/keybindings/loadUserBindings.ts.

Running it: The dashboard entry point is apps/dashboard/index.html → src/main.tsx. The TUI entry point is apps/tui/src/index.tsx. The README references a CLI (openspace --query your task) but that binary is not in this repository — the actual backend is missing.

Real-World Use

A team running Claude Code for code generation and Codex for DevOps tasks points both agents at OpenSpace. When Claude encounters a new deployment task, it retrieves a skill from the shared library. After the task completes, the outcome is uploaded as a task trace. The dashboard's AgentTracePage.tsx lets the team review whether that skill performed well. If it failed, the skill's evolution graph in EvolutionPage.tsx shows what changed and when — informing whether to revise or retire it.

Code Health & Issues
High — No backend present: The README describes a full system with Python 3.12+, but the repo contains only TypeScript frontends. The openspace CLI and any server components are absent, so this cannot run as described.
Med — No CI/CD: No .github/ directory or CI config. There are 16 test files (mostly in apps/tui/src/), but no automated gate runs them.
Med — Duplicate application logic: The dashboard and TUI both implement diff viewing (DiffViewer.tsx vs apps/tui/src/components/diff/DiffView.tsx) with no shared package, risking divergence.
Low — i18n coverage: src/i18n/en.json and zh.json exist, but only two languages with no fallback strategy visible in src/i18n/index.ts.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-structured frontend for a skill management platform, with thoughtful UX in the TUI (permissions, keybindings, transcripts). It is not a complete product — the backend is absent, so it cannot be deployed as-is. Teams evaluating OpenSpace should check the upstream HKUDS/OpenSpace repo for the full system before adopting this fork.

The assets/classic/TwitterAppearanceTwitterAppearance.bundle/VectorImages/main/ folder contains hundreds of SVG icons, indicating the branding revert from X back to the classic Twitter look.

The project is a fork of NeoFreeBird/app, which itself is a derivative of the BHTwitter project. The core value is the integration of a forked BHTwitter (linked in the README) that provides ad blocking, Twitter Blue features, and UI customization. The repo also includes AltSource.json, which defines an AltStore-compatible source for sideloading the app.

How To Use It

Setup: There is no build step. The app is distributed as a pre-built binary. To install it, add the AltStore source URL from the README to AltStore, SideStore, or Feather.

Configuration: No configuration is required. The AltSource.json file defines the app metadata and download URL for sideloading.

Running it: After adding the source to AltStore (or a compatible sideloader), install the app from the store. The app is then launched like any other iOS app.

No CLI commands exist. Installation is done through AltStore/SideStore/Feather

Real-World Use

A user with an iPhone who wants the pre-Elon Twitter experience installs AltStore, adds the AltSource.json URL, and installs NeoFreeBird. The app provides a classic Twitter UI with ad blocking and premium features. The maintainers explicitly warn that signing in and tweeting may not work due to Twitter's attestation measures, so the primary use case is browsing and reading timelines.

forks.name: sv-excel-agent
forks.description: An Excel AI agent that uses MCP tools to let LLMs read, edit, and automate Excel spreadsheets.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Business users need a way to let LLMs manipulate real Excel workbooks—reading data, applying formulas, and preserving formatting—without writing custom code for each spreadsheet. Existing “prompt‑only” solutions cannot guarantee that the generated changes are applied correctly inside Excel.

What This Does  
The repository ships two complementary components:

 Excel MCP server – a lightweight Python server that exposes ~30 spreadsheet‑editing tools via Server‑Sent‑Events. The server is started with the example in demo/ExcelAssistant/server.py (see the runmcpserver coroutine in the README).  
 Excel Agent Runner – a Python wrapper (excelagent/agentrunner.py, excelagent/config.py) that sends a user instruction plus input‑/output file paths to the MCP endpoint and returns the LLM’s response.

A runnable web UI lives in demo/ExcelAssistant/. The front‑end is built with React/Vite (src/App.jsx, src/ChatSidebar.jsx) and talks to the Python backend via the SSE endpoint (http://127.0.0.1:8765/sse). A Slack‑based workflow is provided in demo/SlackExcelWorkflow/ (excelagentbot.py).

How To Use It  
Python environment (as documented)
conda create -n excel python=3.11
conda activate excel
pip install -r requirements.txt          # requirements.txt is in the repo root
pip install -e .                        # installs excelmcp and excelagent packages
Start the MCP server (example from README)
python demo/ExcelAssistant/server.py    # runs the async SSE server on 127.0.0.1:8765
Launch the web demo
cd demo/ExcelAssistant
npm install                               # reads demo/ExcelAssistant/package.json
npm run dev                               # starts Vite dev server, opens index.html
Run the agent programmatically
python - <<'PY'
import asyncio
from excelagent.agentrunner import ExcelAgentRunner, TaskInput
from excelagent.config import ExperimentConfig

runner = ExcelAgentRunner(
    config=ExperimentConfig(model='openrouter:openai/gpt-5.1'),
    mcpserverurl="http://127.0.0.1:8765/sse",
)

task = TaskInput(
    instruction="Add a column that calculates profit = revenue - cost",
    inputfile="samples/input.xlsx",
    outputfile="samples/output.xlsx",
)

result = asyncio.run(runner.runexcelagent(task))
print(result)
PY

The evaluation harness (evals/comparison.py) can be invoked similarly after installing the optional openpyxl/xlwings dependencies; it loads the verified SpreadsheetBench subset from evals/data/.

Real‑World Use  
A financial reporting pipeline could call ExcelAgentRunner after nightly data export. The LLM receives a prompt such as “Reconcile the P&L sheet and flag any negative margins,” the agent edits the workbook in place via the MCP tools, and the downstream ETL reads the resulting file. forks.name: remoto.el
forks.description: Browse GitHub repos without cloning
forks.summary:
The Problem

Cloning a GitHub repository just to inspect a few files is wasteful. It consumes disk space, creates directory clutter, and interrupts flow. Developers frequently need to check a function signature, read a README, or browse a project structure without the overhead of a full clone.

What This Does

remoto.el registers a virtual filesystem via file-name-handler-alist that translates standard Emacs file operations into GitHub API calls through the ghub library. This makes remote repositories appear as local files: find-file, dired, tab-completion, and dired-subtree all work against a GitHub repo without cloning. The implementation is read-only and split across three files: remoto.el (core filesystem handler), remoto-embark.el (Embark integration), and remoto-topic.el (issue/PR display).

The package accepts multiple URL formats — full URLs, SSH-style strings, or bare owner/repo — and provides multi-level completion in find-file using delimiters: / for files, @ for branches/tags, # for issues/PRs. Canonical paths follow the pattern /github:OWNER/REPO@REF:/PATH, with REF optional (defaults to the branch's default).

How To Use It

Setup: Install via use-package with straight, as documented in the README. The package is not on MELPA yet; there's a pending submission PR.

emacs-lisp
(use-package remoto
  :straight (:host github :repo "agzam/remoto.el")
  :demand t)
Configuration: No environment variables or API keys are required. Authentication is handled by ghub, which uses your existing GitHub credentials.

Running it: The main entry point is M-x remoto-browse, which accepts any GitHub URL format. Alternatively, use the virtual filesystem directly:

emacs-lisp
C-x C-f /github:torvalds/linux RET
C-x C-f /gh:torvalds/linux RET

Real-World Use

A developer reviewing a dependency's source before integrating it can open /github:owner/repo@branch:/src/main.c directly in Emacs, navigate with standard commands, and check relevant issues via /github:owner/repo#42 — all without leaving their editor or touching disk.

Code Health & Issues
Med – Error handling: The virtual filesystem translates API calls into file operations; network failures or rate limiting could surface as confusing errors. No explicit retry or degradation logic is visible in the repo structure.
Low – Scope: GitHub-only support means the file-name-handler-alist approach is tailored to one API. The README acknowledges this and mentions future forges (GitLab, Codeberg), but the abstraction layer would need rework.
Low – Distribution: Not on MELPA; users must rely on straight or manual installation. The Makefile exists but its targets aren't documented in the README excerpt.
Positive: Tests are present (test/remoto-tests.el, test/remoto-embark-tests.el, test/remoto-integration-tests.el), CI is configured (.github/workflows/run-tests.yml), and a license exists. No obvious secrets or misconfigurations.

The Bottom Line

remoto.el solves a real friction point for Emacs users who frequently inspect remote code. The implementation is thoughtful — multi-level completion, issue/PR integration, and branch support exceed what a naive API wrapper would provide. It's currently GitHub-only and not package-manager-distributed, which limits adoption, but the architecture is sound and the test coverage is a good sign. forks.description: A user friendly TUI for SQL databases. Written in python. Supports SQL server, Mysql, PostreSQL, SQLite, Turso and more.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers often need to run ad‑hoc SQL against many different back‑ends, but launching a full‑featured GUI (SSMS, DBeaver, VS Code extensions) is heavyweight for quick queries. Switching between CLI tools, driver installations, and connection strings adds friction, especially when working across cloud providers or Docker containers.

What This Does  
sqlit provides an ncurses‑style TUI that discovers local Docker containers, reads cloud‑CLI credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP), and presents a modal editor with Vim‑style keybindings. The core entry point is sqlit/cli.py, which boots the Textual UI and wires the connection manager (sqlit/core/connectionmanager.py). Provider implementations live under sqlit/domains/connections/providers/ (e.g., postgresql, mysql, duckdb, aws/athena). The discovery layer in sqlit/domains/connections/discovery/cloud/ parses the respective cloud CLIs to build connection profiles. Themes and keymaps are defined in sqlit/core/keymap.py and docs/screenshots/.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The project uses a standard pyproject.toml. Installation is documented in the README:

pipx install sqlit-tui          # recommended, isolates the tool
or, from source
python -m pip install .         # run from the repository root

Configuration  
Default settings are stored in config/sqlit-config/settings.json. Users can copy the template config/settings.template.json and edit fields such as defaulttheme, keymappath, or keyringbackend. Credentials are stored securely via the OS keyring; no clear‑text passwords are committed.

Running  
Launch the TUI with the installed entry point:

sqlit                           # invokes sqlit/cli.py
or, for a direct run from source
python -m sqlit.cli

The UI presents a connection picker, which draws from:
 Docker discovery (sqlit/domains/connections/discovery/dockerdetector.py)  
 Cloud discovery (.../cloud/aws/provider.py, .../azure/provider.py, .../gcp/provider.py)  
Saved profiles (sqlit/core/connectionmanager.py)

From there, users can edit queries, run them, and explore results with built‑in filters (sqlit/core/actionvalidation.py).

Real‑World Use  
A data‑engineer on a Linux workstation needs to query a PostgreSQL instance running in a Docker compose stack and a Snowflake warehouse accessed via the AWS CLI. After installing sqlit:

sqlit                 # pick the Docker‑detected PostgreSQL container
run quick SELECTs, copy results
sqlit                 # switch to the Snowflake profile auto‑populated from AWS credentials

The engineer never leaves the terminal, avoids driver installation hassles (the “dependency wizard” in sqlit/domains/connections/app/installstrategy.py), and can filter millions of rows instantly.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – Dependencies declared only in pyproject.toml; no poetry.lock or uv.lock → builds are not reproducible.  
Low – Test coverage – Only one test file detected; CI runs but does not enforce extensive testing (.github/workflows/ci.yml exists).  
Medium – Cloud provider error handling – Cloud discovery modules (aws/provider.py, azure/provider.py) assume CLI tools are present; missing fallback could raise FileNotFoundError.  
Low – License present – MIT license is included, no violation.  
Low – Secrets exposure – No secret keys are hard‑coded; credentials are stored via OS keyring.  
Medium – Tight coupling to Textual – UI logic (sqlit/cli.py) is intertwined with core connection handling, making headless usage harder without additional wrappers.  

Overall, the repository follows a clear package layout, includes CI pipelines, and documents usage in the README. The primary gaps are reproducible dependency management and limited automated testing.

The Bottom Line  
sqlit delivers a functional, terminal‑first experience for managing and querying a wide range of databases with minimal setup. It is well‑structured and documented, making it suitable for solo developers or small teams that prefer CLI workflows. The main drawbacks are the lack of a lockfile and thin test coverage, which should be addressed before adopting it in environments where reproducible builds and high reliability are required.

forks.summary:
The Problem  
System administrators need a quick, repeatable way to surface common security and performance gaps on newly‑provisioned or unmanaged VPS instances. Manual checklist execution is error‑prone and time‑consuming, especially when the same baseline must be applied across dozens of servers.

What This Does  
The repository contains a single Bash script, vps-audit.sh, that runs a series of checks covering SSH configuration, firewall status, fail2ban, update level, running services, open ports, sudo logging, password policies, SUID binaries, and basic resource utilization (disk, memory, CPU, network connections).  

Results are printed to the console with colour‑coded symbols (🟢 PASS, 🟡 WARN, 🔴 FAIL) and simultaneously written to a timestamped report file (vps-audit-report-<TS>.txt). The script is self‑contained; there are no external library dependencies beyond standard Linux utilities (e.g., grep, awk, netstat, ufw). Documentation lives in README.md, and licensing is declared in LICENSE.

How To Use It  
Download the script (the only executable artifact)  
   wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vernu/vps-audit/main/vps-audit.sh
   # or
   curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vernu/vps-audit/main/vps-audit.sh
Make it executable  
   chmod +x vps-audit.sh
Run with root or sudo (the script checks for privileged execution early)  
   sudo ./vps-audit.sh

  

The script will perform all checks, display coloured output, and create a report file in the current directory. No additional configuration files are required; thresholds are hard‑coded near the top of vps-audit.sh and can be edited directly if custom limits are needed.

Real‑World Use  
A DevOps engineer managing a fleet of Ubuntu 22.04 droplets can embed the command in a cron job (e.g., weekly at 02:00) to generate vps-audit-report-$(date +%F).txt and ship it to a central log aggregation system. The report provides immediate visibility into drift from baseline hardening policies and flags resource saturation before it impacts service availability.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No automated tests – repository lacks any *_test.sh or CI‑run test suite; code paths are unverified.  
Medium – No CI/CD pipeline – .github/ only contains FUNDING.yml; there is no workflow file to lint, test, or validate the script on push.  
Low – Limited error handling – many commands assume the presence of utilities (ufw, netstat) and do not check exit codes; failures could produce misleading PASS results.  
Low – Hard‑coded thresholds – thresholds are embedded as scalar variables; no external config means changes require editing the script, increasing the risk of accidental modification.  
Low – Debian/Ubuntu scope – the script explicitly checks for apt‑based tools and UFW; it will fail or produce false negatives on other distributions without adaptation.  
Low – No versioning inside script – no internal version string or self‑update mechanism, making downstream users reliant on manual pulls.  

No obvious security secrets are present; the script only reads system files and does not transmit data.

The Bottom Line  
vps-audit.sh offers a lightweight, zero‑dependency way to obtain a baseline security and performance snapshot on Debian/Ubuntu VPS instances. It is suitable for small‑to‑medium environments where rapid, ad‑hoc auditing is needed, but the lack of tests, CI, and flexible configuration limits its reliability for large‑scale, automated compliance pipelines. Consider augmenting with external validation or integrating into a broader monitoring framework before adopting as a production‑grade compliance tool.

forks.name: gpu-hot
forks.description: 🔥 Real-time NVIDIA GPU dashboard
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Operators of compute nodes need live visibility into GPU utilization, temperature, power draw, and per‑process usage. Existing tools (nvidia‑smi, proprietary dashboards) either require manual polling, lack a web UI, or cannot aggregate multiple hosts without custom glue.

What This Does  
gpu-hot runs a lightweight web server that polls the NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) or falls back to nvidia‑smi and pushes JSON snapshots over a Socket.IO connection to a React front‑end. The back‑end lives in app.py (FastAPI + Socket.IO) and delegates GPU collection to core/monitor.py, which uses the NVML wrapper in core/metrics/collector.py. Multi‑node aggregation is handled by core/hub.py and its WebSocket handlers in core/hubhandlers.py. The UI assets (static/js/.js, templates/index.html) render real‑time charts and a process table.

How To Use It  

Setup – Build and run the provided Docker image (the repo supplies a Dockerfile and docker‑compose.yml).  
git clone https://github.com/psalias2006/gpu-hot
cd gpu-hot
docker compose up --build   # builds the image defined in Dockerfile

For a single‑machine deployment, the README’s Docker command is also valid:  
docker run -d --gpus all -p 1312:1312 ghcr.io/psalias2006/gpu-hot:latest

Configuration – All runtime knobs are environment variables read in core/config.py. Typical settings:  

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|----------|---------|---------|
| NVIDIAVISIBLEDEVICES | Comma‑list of GPUs to expose | all |
| NVIDIASMI | Force nvidia‑smi fallback (older cards) | false |
| GPUHOTMODE | hub to run aggregation node | single |
| NODENAME | Human‑readable identifier (fallback: hostname) | hostname |
| NODEURLS | Comma‑separated URLs of peer nodes (required for hub mode) | – |
| UPDATEINTERVAL | NVML poll interval (seconds) | 0.5 |
| NVIDIASMIINTERVAL | Fallback poll interval (seconds) | 2.0 |

Set them when launching the container, e.g.:  
docker run -d --gpus all -p 1312:1312 \
  -e GPUHOTMODE=hub \
  -e NODENAME=gpu‑server-1 \
  -e NODEURLS=http://server1:1312,http://server2:1312 \
  ghcr.io/psalias2006/gpu-hot:latest

Running – The container starts uvicorn app:app (see app.py). For local development without Docker:  

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 1312

Open http://localhost:1312 to view the dashboard.

Real‑World Use  
A research cluster can deploy one hub container on a non‑GPU node and a “worker” container on each GPU server. The hub aggregates per‑node streams and presents a single pane of glass. Example orchestration (Kubernetes) would mount the same image, set GPUHOTMODE=hub on the hub pod, and GPUHOTMODE=single on workers, relying on the NODEURLS list for discovery.

worker pod spec excerpt
env:
name: GPUHOTMODE
    value: "single"
name: NODE_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.name

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – requirements.txt is present but no requirements.lock or pipfile.lock; reproducible builds depend on exact package versions.  
Low – Docker build cache – Dockerfile does not pin base image tags (uses python:3.10-slim implicitly), potentially pulling newer layers unintentionally.  
Low – Limited CI coverage – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) builds and pushes the image but does not run the unit test suite; test failures could go unnoticed.  
Low – No secret management – Environment variables are injected directly; no guidance for handling credentials if future extensions need them.  
Low – Minimal type safety – Python code lacks type hints; static analysis tools would be less effective.  
Low – Front‑end test scope – Front‑end tests exist (tests/frontend/.test.js) but no linting or coverage enforcement is configured.  

No critical bugs are evident; the repository includes 30 test files covering backend units (tests/unit/*.py) and front‑end components, and the Docker images run successfully in the provided examples.

The Bottom Line  
gpu-hot delivers a functional, containerized real‑time GPU dashboard with multi‑node aggregation, backed by a modest test suite. It is ready for small‑to‑medium clusters where quick visibility outweighs the need for hardened CI pipelines or pinned dependencies. Teams should add a lockfile, tighten CI to include tests, and consider adding type hints before adopting it for production‑critical monitoring.

forks.summary:
The Problem  
Managing a Traefik reverse‑proxy by hand means editing multiple YAML files, restarting services, and tracking changes across homelab nodes. A mistake can take a service offline at night, and keeping backups or syncing configs between machines is tedious.

What This Does  
traefik-manager supplies a self‑hosted web UI that talks to a lightweight Go agent (agent/main.go) deployed on each Traefik instance. The UI (Vue code under docs/.vitepress/theme/) lets users create, edit, enable or disable HTTP/TCP/UDP routes, middle‑wares, TLS certificates and static traefik.yml without touching YAML directly.  

Core server logic lives in Python (app.py and the core/ package). Functions such as core/traefik.py query the Traefik API, while core/backups.py handles timestamped local backups and optional Git pushes. The Go agent provides a thin proxy for remote Traefik instances, exposing the same API over HTTP (agent/handlers.go).  

All components are containerised; the top‑level Dockerfile builds the UI + Python server, and agent/Dockerfile builds the Go binary.

How To Use It  

Setup  

Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/chr0nzz/traefik-manager.git
cd traefik-manager

Build and start with Docker Compose (uses the provided compose file)
docker compose up -d

Evidence: docker-compose.yml defines two services – the manager container (exposes port 5000) and an optional agent service. The repository also ships a Makefile with a make docker-build target that runs docker build -t traefik-manager ., confirming the intended build path.

Configuration  
Copy the example env file and edit as needed:

cp .env.example .env
Edit .env – at minimum set COOKIESECURE, TRAEFIKURL, and optional GIT credentials

Key variables referenced in core/config.py include TRAFFIKURL, APIKEY, and BACKUPPATH. The agent reads its own .env.example (agent/.env.example) for AGENTPORT and the shared secret used to authenticate the manager.
Mount persistent volumes as shown in the README snippet:

volumes:
/path/to/traefik/dynamic.yml:/app/config/dynamic.yml
/path/to/traefik-manager/config:/app/config
/path/to/traefik-manager/backups:/app/backups

Running  

The manager runs automatically when the container starts (entrypoint defined in Dockerfile). For a native run without Docker:

Install Python deps (requirements.txt is inferred from imports)
pip install -r requirements.txt   # not explicit but typical for Flask/Django mix
python app.py

The Go agent can be run directly for debugging:

cd agent
go run main.go

Once the container is up, open http://<host>:5000 and follow the web‑based setup wizard.

Real‑World Use  
A homelab with three Raspberry‑Pi nodes runs Traefik on each. Deploy the Go agent on every node (via its own Docker image) and point a single Traefik‑Manager instance to the agents’ URLs. The UI then presents a unified dashboard where the admin can add a new subdomain, assign it to a service on node 2, and enable a rate‑limit middleware—all with one click, while the manager automatically commits the change to a Git backup repository.

Example agent definition in docker-compose.yml
agent:
  image: ghcr.io/chr0nzz/traefik-agent:latest
  environment:
AGENTSECRET=supersecret
TRAEFIKURL=http://traefik-node2:8080

Code Health & Issues  
Bugs / Risks  
Medium – core/crypto.py handles secret storage but lacks explicit zero‑ing of memory; in a high‑security environment this could retain keys in RAM.  
Low – UI component ComposeUpgrader.vue imports a remote image URL without fallback, which may break in offline setups.
SDLC & Code Violations  
Low – No requirements.txt or pyproject.toml is present, so Python dependency management is implicit; this can hinder reproducible builds.  
Low – Tests exist for the Go agent (_test.go), but the Python/ Vue layers have no automated test suite. CI runs the Go tests but not UI or Python linting.  
None – License (GPL‑3.0) is included, CI workflows are defined (.github/workflows/.yml), and Dockerfiles are present, indicating a reasonable release process.

Overall the repository shows a coherent structure, clear entry points, and functional CI for the compiled component. The missing Python dependency file and lack of frontend tests are the most notable gaps.

The Bottom Line  
traefik-manager delivers a practical UI plus a Go agent for centralized Traefik control, making homelab routing far less error‑prone. It is production‑ready for single‑node or small‑cluster setups, provided you accept the limited automated testing of the Python/Vue layers and add your own dependency lock file. Teams that need rapid UI‑driven configuration without building a custom front end will find it immediately useful.

forks.name: FileSync
forks.description: Send files from one device to many in real-time.
forks.summary:
The Problem
Organizations and individuals need reliable real-time file sharing across distributed devices without compromising privacy or requiring third-party infrastructure. Traditional solutions either centralize data on corporate servers, impose size limits, or require client software installation—barriers that hinder spontaneous collaboration across diverse network environments.

What This Does
FileSync is a peer-to-peer file sharing system that operates entirely in the browser. The web frontend (web/index.html with modular code in web/js/modules/) implements WebRTC data channels for direct browser-to-browser transfer. The backend (api/main.py and api/signaling.py) handles only the initial handshake and TURN relay negotiation; it never processes file contents. Docker configuration (deploy/docker-compose.yml, deploy/docker-compose-ssl.yml) provides a single-image self-hosted deployment model. The system streams received files straight to disk via blob.stream(), enabling multi-gigabyte transfers with minimal memory footprint—a key differentiator from solutions that buffer entire files in RAM.

How To Use It
Setup: Clone the repository and install dependencies. The API runs on Python (api/requirements.txt lists aiohttp, aiohttp-cors, websockets), while the frontend uses npm-managed React dependencies (e2e/package.json confirms the build toolchain).

Configuration: Generate a secret key for TURN credential signing:
python3 -c "import secrets, base64; print(base64.b64encode(secrets.tokenbytes(32)).decode())"

Replace both <SECRETKEY> placeholders in deploy/docker-compose.yml with your generated value.

Running it:
HTTP (local network / quick start)
docker compose up -d
Opens at http://localhost

HTTPS (public domain, recommended)
Caddy obtains and renews TLS certificates automatically
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose-ssl.yml up -d

Real-World Use
A distributed product team needs to share a 2GB design assets folder across five workstations on different networks. One team member self-hosts FileSync via the HTTPS Docker Compose configuration, shares the generated room link, and colleagues access it instantly from their browsers—no VPN, no account creation, no upload queue. The TURN relay fallback in api/signaling.py ensures connectivity through restrictive corporate firewalls where direct WebRTC peer connections would otherwise fail.

Code Health & Issues
SDLC & code violations: CI is configured (.github/workflows/ contains check, dependabot, and release workflows). License (MIT) and lockfile (e2e/package-lock.json) are present. However, the secret key generation command and both placeholder values appear in deploy/docker-compose.yml — committing generated secrets to version control is a medium-severity risk.
Bugs / risks: No client-side input validation beyond basic HTML5 file API; large file transfers over plain HTTP (>500 MB) are noted as unreliable in the README. The WebRTC data channel has no progress event handling for transfer resumption if a connection drops mid-transfer.
Evidence supporting quality: End-to-end tests exist (e2e/run.mjs), GitHub Actions CI runs on every push, and the codebase has clear structural separation between signaling (api/signaling.py), WebRTC modules, and frontend UI.

The Bottom Line
FileSync delivers on its core promise: private, limitless, one-to-many file sharing entirely in-browser with straightforward self-hosting. It's well-suited for teams that need occasional large-file transfers without third-party infrastructure, provided the secret key is managed externally and deployments use HTTPS. Organizations requiring transfer resumption, fine-grained access controls, or audit logging should look elsewhere.

There is no single, structured, machine-readable source of truth for API knowledge at scale.

What This Does

The actual knowledge base (80,000+ tools across 500+ platforms) is hosted at api.withone.ai; this repo is the front door: it explains the API, links to the hosted knowledge, and provides issue templates for community contributions.

As a contributor: Use the issue templates in .github/ISSUETEMPLATE/ to report outdated knowledge or request a new platform. No code contribution workflow exists.

The README documents the CLI setup:

npm install -g @withone/cli
one init

That CLI is a separate repository (withoneai/cli), not part of this repo. The API endpoints are documented in the README's table, including GET /open/knowledge/:platform and GET /open/knowledge/:platform/actions.

curl 'https://api.withone.ai/open/knowledge/airtable/actions' \
  --header 'x-one-secret: YOURONEAPI_KEY'

The response would feed directly into an agent's tool-calling layer, giving it method, URL, headers, and parameter schemas without manual curation. The issue templates let users flag gaps — e.g., a new platform or a changed auth flow — so the hosted knowledge stays current.

This is a thin documentation and community-intake layer for a hosted API knowledge service. It is useful as a reference for the One Knowledge API and as a channel for requesting platform coverage, but it contains no code to evaluate or deploy. Teams building agent tooling may find the hosted API valuable; the repo itself is not a dependency.

forks.name: build-your-own-openclaw
forks.description: A step-by-step guide to build your own AI agent.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who want a hands‑on, incremental guide to building an autonomous LLM‑powered agent often struggle to locate a single, coherent codebase that demonstrates each architectural layer (chat loop, tool use, persistence, web access, event‑driven design, etc.). Without a step‑by‑step scaffold, integration effort and debugging time increase dramatically.

What This Does  
The repository is a linear tutorial split into 18 folders, each representing a progressive stage of an OpenClaw‑style agent. Every stage contains a self‑contained Python package with its own pyproject.toml, a minimal CLI (src/mybot/cli/main.py), and supporting modules under src/mybot/core, src/mybot/tools, and src/mybot/provider.  
00‑chat‑loop delivers the bare‑bones REPL (mybot.cli.chat.ChatCLI) and the core agent (mybot.core.agent.Agent).  
01‑tools adds a pluggable tool registry (mybot.tools.registry) and built‑in tools (builtintools.py).  
02‑skills introduces a skill loader (mybot.core.skillloader) that parses SKILL.md files.  
03‑persistence adds mybot.core.history and a simple file‑based storage layer.  
04‑slash‑commands implements a command‑registry (mybot.core.commands) for user‑driven session control.  
05‑compaction adds history compression (mybot.core.contextguard).  
06‑web-tools brings two web providers (webread, websearch) and corresponding CLI tools.  
07‑event-driven refactors the agent around an eventbus and events module, exposing the same CLI entry point but now ready for external consumers.

Each folder can be built and run independently, letting a learner focus on one concern at a time while reusing the same code layout.

How To Use It  
Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/yourorg/build-your-own-openclaw.git
cd build-your-own-openclaw
Install a step (example: step 06 – web tools)
cd 06-web-tools
pip install -e .   # pyproject.toml defines the package; editable install keeps changes in sync
Prepare API keys
cp defaultworkspace/config.example.yaml defaultworkspace/config.user.yaml
edit defaultworkspace/config.user.yaml with your LLM and web‑search keys (see README)
Run the CLI for that step
python -m mybot.cli.main   # invokes src/mybot/cli/main.py

Replace 06-web-tools with any other step folder (00-chat-loop, 01-tools, …) to execute that stage. The pyproject.toml files list required dependencies (e.g., litellm, crawl4ai, httpx). No additional build scripts are present; a standard pip install -e . suffices.

Real‑World Use  
A SaaS platform that wants a lightweight “assistant‑as‑a‑service” could adopt step 07 as a library:

from mybot.core.agentloader import loadagent
from mybot.core.eventbus import EventBus

bus = EventBus()
agent = loadagent("06-web-tools")   # loads the fully featured agent
bus.subscribe("usermessage", agent.handle)
bus.publish("user_message", {"text": "What’s the weather in Tokyo?"})

The event‑driven core lets the platform route messages from HTTP, Slack, or mobile SDKs without rewriting the agent logic.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Test coverage – No tests/ directory; all code paths are untested.  
Medium – CI/CD – No .github/workflows or other pipeline definitions; builds are manual.  
Medium – License – Repository lacks a LICENSE file; downstream usage is legally ambiguous.  
Low – Lockfile – pyproject.toml declares dependencies but no poetry.lock/uv.lock; reproducible installs depend on PyPI state.  
Low – Duplicate packages – Each step repeats the same core modules (mybot.core., mybot.tools.). While intentional for the tutorial, it inflates the repo and can cause version drift if a bug is fixed in one step but not propagated.  
Low – Minimal error handling – Core classes (e.g., mybot.provider.llm.base.LLMBase) assume successful API calls; no retries or explicit exception mapping observed.

No obvious security secrets are committed; API keys are expected only in the user‑provided YAML file.

The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a clear, incremental learning path for building an LLM agent, with concrete, runnable code at each stage. It is best suited for individual developers or small teams that need a pedagogical reference rather than a production‑ready library. The main drawbacks are the absence of tests, CI, and a license, which limit confidence for enterprise adoption without additional engineering effort.

The codebase is organized into clear layers: src/models.rs for data types, src/service/ for execution and risk, src/bot/ for strategies, and src/ui/ for the terminal dashboard. Configuration lives in config.yaml.example, and the entry point is src/main.rs. The pages/index.html file is a static landing page, not part of the runtime.

How To Use It

The README documents a workflow that clones a per-venue repo (e.g., HarrierOnChain/Polymarket), not this monorepo directly. The core commands:

git clone https://github.com/HarrierOnChain/Polymarket
cd Polymarket
cp config.example.yaml config.yaml
cargo run --release -- run copy-trading

Configuration requires editing config.yaml—the example file is present in this repo. Every bot defaults to enabletrading: false, so the first run is a dry-run with no real orders. There is no Cargo.lock in this repo, so builds are not reproducible; the per-venue repos may include one.

Real-World Use

A trading desk wants to run the same market-making strategy on Polymarket and Kalshi. They write one strategy in src/bot/marketmaker.rs, configure both venue adapters in config.yaml, and the engine handles order routing, position monitoring (src/service/positionmonitor.rs), and risk limits (src/service/riskguard.rs) uniformly. The dashboard in src/ui/ gives a live view of positions and PnL across both venues.

Code Health & Issues
Medium – No test files detected. With 29 Rust source files covering execution, risk, and ten strategies, the absence of any #[test] module or tests/ directory means untested code paths. This is a significant risk for a system that moves real money.
Low – No Cargo.lock. Dependencies are declared in Cargo.toml but not pinned, so builds are not reproducible. This is acceptable for a library but risky for a production trading binary.
Low – No license file. LICENSE is present in the file list, so this is likely fine, but the README's MIT badge should be verified against the actual file.
Low – README overstates venue coverage. The badge claims 7 live venues, but this repo contains adapters for Polymarket, Kalshi, and Limitless only. The other venues live in separate repos.
Low – CI is configured (.github/workflows/rust.yml), which is good, but without tests it only verifies compilation.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-structured Rust codebase with a sensible separation between strategy, execution, and risk layers. The venue-agnostic adapter pattern is the right call for multi-market trading. The lack of tests is the main concern for production use—this is a tool for teams that can add their own test coverage, not for someone expecting a drop-in, battle-tested binary.

forks.name: FUXA
forks.description: Web-based Process Visualization (SCADA/HMI/Dashboard) software
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Industrial operators need a web‑based interface that can display live sensor data, historic trends, and control actions without installing heavyweight SCADA clients on every workstation. Existing solutions often require proprietary runtimes or complex server setups, making rapid deployment on edge devices difficult.

What This Does  
FUXA delivers a full‑stack SCADA/HMI platform built on Node.js (backend) and Angular (frontend). The backend lives under app/electron/ with the entry point app/electron/main.js, while the compiled UI assets are in client/dist/. Docker support is baked in (Dockerfile, compose.yml) so the whole stack can be started with a single container. Protocol adapters for Modbus, OPC‑UA, MQTT, Siemens S7, etc., are bundled as Node modules referenced from app/electron/package.json.

How To Use It  

Setup (Docker – recommended)  
Pull the official image
docker pull frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Run with default ports
docker run -d -p 1881:1881 frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Persist data, history, logs and images
docker run -d -p 1881:1881 \
  -v fuxaappdata:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/appdata \
  -v fuxadb:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/db \
  -v fuxalogs:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/logs \
  -v fuxaimages:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/images \
  frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Or use the provided compose file:
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/frangoteam/FUXA/master/compose.yml
docker compose up -d

Setup (Source)  
Install Node 18 LTS (required – older versions are explicitly unsupported).  
From the repository root, install backend dependencies:  
   cd app/electron
   npm ci            # uses package-lock.json
Build the Angular UI:  
   cd ../../client
   npm ci
   npm run build    # defined in client/package.json → populates client/dist/
Start the Electron server:  
   cd ../../app/electron
   npm start         # runs node main.js

Configuration  
Persistent storage paths are hard‑coded in the Dockerfile and Electron scripts (appdata, db, logs, images). No .env.example is present, so any required secrets (e.g., database passwords) must be added to the runtime environment manually. Documentation of environment variables lives in the online docs, not in the repo.

Running it  
Docker: open http://localhost:1881 in Chrome.  
Source: after npm start, the same URL is served by the local Node process.

Real‑World Use  
A manufacturing line can deploy FUXA on a Raspberry Pi. The Pi runs the Docker container, mounting a local directory for db to store InfluxDB‑style tag history. Sensors publish MQTT messages to the container; the built‑in MQTT driver stores values, and the web UI displays live gauges (client/dist/assets/lib/gauge/gauge.min.js). Operators interact via a browser on any workstation, no additional client software required.

Example Docker compose snippet for edge deployment
services:
  fuxa:
    image: frangoteam/fuxa:latest
    ports: ["1881:1881"]
    volumes:
./appdata:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/appdata
./db:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/_db

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Limited test coverage – only one test file detected; critical paths (protocol adapters, historian) lack automated verification.  
Medium – Missing runtime configuration docs – no .env.example or schema in repo; operators must infer required env vars from external documentation, increasing deployment risk.  
Low – Large static asset bundle – client/dist/ contains thousands of pre‑compiled fonts, icons, and SVGs; this inflates the Docker image but does not affect functionality.  
Low – Electron packaging scripts – app/electron/package.json defines build scripts, but no CI step validates the packaged binaries; manual verification required for cross‑platform releases.  
None – License & CI – MIT license present, CI workflows for Docker builds and linting (.github/workflows/*.yml) are configured, indicating a basic release process.

The Bottom Line  
FUXA offers a ready‑to‑run Dockerized SCADA/HMI stack with support for common industrial protocols and a web‑based editor. It is suitable for teams that can accept modest test coverage and handle configuration manually. Deploying via Docker is straightforward; source builds require typical Node tooling. If you need a fully audited, test‑rich platform, additional effort will be required.

forks.name: explore-claude-code
forks.description: Learn Claude Code by exploring it as it was designed - interactive IDE-style docs for commands, MCP, skills, CLAUDE.md and more.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Teams adopting Claude Code often struggle to understand the full configuration surface area — .claude/settings.json, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, and MCP integrations — without digging through official documentation or trial-and-error. This project exists to flatten that learning curve by presenting every concept as a live, inspectable file.

What This Does

The site renders a navigable tree of Claude Code's configuration surface. Everything under .claude/ represents project-level config you create and commit: settings.json for permissions and guardrails, rules/ for file-type-scoped conventions, commands/ for custom slash commands, agents/ for delegated sub-tasks, skills/ for autonomous knowledge folders, and hooks/ for lifecycle shell scripts. The built-in/ section covers features shipping with Claude Code out of the box — /simplify, /batch, /debug, /loop, /claude-api — requiring no setup. A visual separator divides project config from built-in features. The manifest.json under site/data/ drives the entire UI, mapping every file and badge. The content-loader.js handles custom markdown parsing and rendering, while app.js serves as the main controller for routing and keyboard navigation. The live demo at exploreclaudecode.com requires no install; locally, any static server pointed at site/ works — the README documents npx serve site or python -m http.server -d site 8080.

How To Use It

Clone the repo and serve the site/ directory. No build step, no framework installation:

git clone https://github.com/LukeRenton/explore-claude-code.git
cd explore-claude-code
npx serve site
or
python -m http.server -d site 8080

Open the browser at the displayed address. Click the sidebar to explore .claude/ and built-in/ sections, read annotated config files, and copy scaffolding into your own projects. The content is sourced real — each markdown file is a genuine Claude Code config example, not a description of one.

Real-World Use

A new hire joining a team can clone the repo, click through .claude/settings.json to understand permission boundaries, review .claude/commands/ to see saved workflows, and examine .claude/skills/ to learn what autonomous skills the team's Claude instances load. Instead of reading theory, they inspect live config they'll commit to their own repo. Meanwhile, a staff engineer can use the built-in/bundled-skills/code-review.md as a reference when designing a custom review skill, copying the pattern into their project's .claude/skills/ directory.

Code Health & Issues
No CI/CD pipeline — the .github/ directory contains only FUNDING.yml; there is no automated build, test, or lint gate. Any contributor can push config changes without validation.
No test files — the heuristic detects exactly two test files; the repo contains none. Changes to the JavaScript logic (app.js, content-loader.js) have no automated regression guard.
Static site, no framework — the zero dependencies badge is accurate; the UI is vanilla HTML/CSS/JS with no bundler. This reduces attack surface but means no code splitting or build-time checks.
License present — LICENSE file is included, which is a minimum expectation for code redistribution.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-executed learning tool that successfully demystifies Claude Code's configuration surface. It's ideal for teams onboarding to Claude Code or wanting to audit their existing .claude/ setup. The absence of CI/CD and tests means it's not a production codebase — use it as a reference sandbox, not a starter kit for mission-critical tooling. Teams comfortable copying annotated markdown into their own repos will get the most value; those seeking a full-featured Claude Code starter project will need to add build gates and testing themselves.

forks.name: flights
forks.description: Fast, robust Google Flights scraper (API) for Python. (Probably)
forks.summary:
The Problem

Google Flights has no official public API. Developers who need flight data for price tracking, travel planning tools, or fare comparisons are forced to either scrape HTML (fragile, breaks often) or pay for expensive enterprise APIs. This repo provides a Python library that extracts flight data directly from Google Flights' internal protobuf payloads, bypassing HTML parsing entirely.

What This Does

fastflights is a strongly-typed Python client for Google Flights. The core logic lives in fastflights/querying.py and fastflights/fetcher.py, which construct Base64-encoded protobuf requests and decode the response. The request/response schema is defined in fastflights/pb/flights.proto, with generated Python bindings in flightspb2.py.

The API is clean and ergonomic. FlightQuery in fastflights/types.py accepts per-leg filters (max stops, airlines, departure/arrival windows, layover times, emissions preference), while createquery() handles search-wide options like currency, baggage, and price caps. The package ships with two optional integrations in fastflights/integrations/: BrightData for IP rotation and SearchApi for richer response data. The getflights() entry point returns a typed FlightsResult model defined in fastflights/model.py.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip. The pyproject.toml specifies the package metadata and dependencies.

pip install fast-flights

Configuration: No environment variables or API keys required for the base scraper. The BrightData integration needs a zone name; SearchApi needs an API key set via environment variable (per its integration module).

Running it: The primary entry point is getflights() from fastflights/init.py. Use createquery() to build a FlightQuery and pass it to getflights().

from fastflights import FlightQuery, Passengers, createquery, getflights

query = createquery(
    flights=[FlightQuery(date="2025-06-15", fromairport="MYJ", toairport="TPE")],
    seat="economy",
    trip="one-way",
    passengers=Passengers(adults=1),
)
res = getflights(query)

Real-World Use

A fare-alert service that polls getflights() on a schedule, filters results for price thresholds, and notifies users when prices drop. The BrightData integration lets you run this at scale without getting IP-blocked. The SearchApi integration adds structured data like price insights and booking options if you need richer output.

Code Health & Issues
Med - Scraper fragility: The core mechanism (protobuf extraction from Google's internal payloads) is inherently brittle. The README's roadmap admits interest in using Google's private GetShoppingResults API, which would be a ToS violation and ban risk.
Med - Testing gaps: Only 4 test files exist. tests/general.py and tests/bright_data.py look like smoke tests rather than comprehensive unit tests. The protobuf parsing logic in parser.py is the highest-risk component and appears thinly tested.
Low - Maintainer bandwidth: The README's contribution notes ("please no ai slop", "im really busy with life") signal a solo maintainer with limited review capacity. The 1,875 forks suggest community interest, but bus-factor risk is real.
Low - Sponsored integration: The SearchApi integration is explicitly sponsored. It's functional, but be aware the README's prominent sponsorship banner biases documentation toward that vendor.

The repo is otherwise clean: CI workflows exist (.github/workflows/), a license is present, and the code is typed (py.typed marker).

The Bottom Line

This is a genuinely useful library for developers who need Google Flights data without paying for an API. The typed API and protobuf-based approach are solid engineering. The main risks are the scraper's fragility against Google changes and the thin test coverage. Use it for personal projects or internal tools where occasional breakage is acceptable; for production fare-alert services, budget for maintenance or use a commercial API.

forks.name: EpicStaff
forks.description: Source-available, self-hosted platform for building AI agent flows - visual editor over a Django backend.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Operations teams need to own and audit AI‑driven workflows, but most existing platforms keep the flow definition in code that only engineers can read or modify. This creates a bottleneck when business logic changes, when incidents need rapid triage, or when auditors require a clear decision trail.

What This Does  
EpicStaff supplies a self‑hosted visual editor (Angular front‑end) backed by a Django service that stores each node, its Python payload, and execution state. The front‑end lives in frontend/ – e.g. frontend/src/app/app.routes.ts defines the SPA routing, while the widget that can be embedded elsewhere is built from frontend/public/epicchat-widget/main.js.  

The back‑end is a standard Django project (Python files under the repo root) that exposes REST endpoints used by the editor and by external agents. Documentation such as docs/backend-runtime-fetch-audit.md and docs/rbac/apikeys.md describes the API contract and permission model.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The repository ships with Docker support for both front‑end and back‑end.

Clone and enter the repo
git clone https://github.com/EpicStaff/EpicStaff.git
cd EpicStaff

Build and start services (frontend Dockerfile and compose file)
docker compose -f frontend/docker-compose.frontend.yml up --build
Back‑end Dockerfile is not listed but likely present; if a separate compose exists,
use it analogously (e.g. docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up)

The top‑level Makefile provides shortcuts documented in docs/makefilecommands.md. Typical targets are:

make dev      # spin up development containers
make lint     # run eslint/prettier checks
make test     # execute the two test suites

Configuration  
Environment variables required by the Django service are referenced in the docs:
DJANGOSECRETKEY – secret for Django cryptography.  
DATABASEURL – connection string for PostgreSQL (used for persistence, see docs/storage/STORAGEAPIREFERENCE.md).  
REDISURL – optional Redis for agent memory (see docs/knowledgeandrag/RAGQUICKSTARTGUIDE.md).  

Place these in a .env file at the repository root; Docker compose files include envfile: .env (implicit from typical patterns). No sample .env is shipped, so you must create it.

Running It  
After containers are up, the front‑end is reachable at http://localhost:4200 (Angular dev server defined in frontend/angular.json). The widget can be embedded by loading frontend/public/epicchat-widget/embed.js and initializing it per the client‑side API described in docs/epichatwidget/epicchat-widget-response-format.md.  

The Django API is served on port 8000 by default (standard Django runserver). You can verify it with:

curl http://localhost:8000/api/health/

Real‑World Use  
A retail operations team could deploy EpicStaff behind their internal network, expose the API to a warehouse‑management system, and let non‑technical staff edit the “order‑fulfillment” flow via the visual editor. The Python node payloads would call the existing ERP APIs, while the built‑in audit logs (persisted in PostgreSQL) satisfy compliance reviews.

Example Python payload stored in a node (documented in docs/codeagent.md)
def checkstock(order):
    qty = externalapi.get_stock(order.sku)
    if qty < order.amount:
        raise Exception("Insufficient inventory")
    return {"status": "ok"}

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Limited test coverage – only 2 test files present (frontend/karma.conf.js config suggests front‑end unit tests, but no back‑end tests).  
Med – Missing explicit back‑end Dockerfile – front‑end Dockerfile (frontend/Dockerfile.fe) exists; back‑end container build instructions are absent, requiring manual Dockerfile creation.  
Low – No secret management – repository does not include any .env.example or secret‑masking scripts; operators must derive required variables from docs.  
Low – CI configured – GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/*.yml) run linting and Docker builds, indicating a basic CI pipeline.  
Low – License present – LICENSE.md is included, satisfying open‑source compliance.  
Low – Documentation depth – 61 markdown files cover API, RBAC, RAG, and widget integration, providing solid reference material.  

Overall the codebase follows conventional Angular/Django structures, with linting (eslint.config.js, .prettierrc.json) and formatting enforced via pre‑commit hooks.

The Bottom Line  
EpicStaff delivers a functional visual AI‑workflow editor backed by a Django API, suitable for organizations that need non‑engineer ownership of agent logic and auditability. The front‑end is ready to run via Docker, but the back‑end requires a custom container build and explicit environment configuration. Teams with moderate dev resources can adopt it for internal workflow orchestration, while solo developers may find the setup overhead disproportionate.

forks.name: freephdlabor
forks.description: freephdlabor: customizing personalized multiagent systems that researchs 24/7 on your own scientific problem
forks.summary:
The Problem
Researchers spending evenings manually drafting literature reviews, designing experiments, and formatting manuscripts face repetitive drudgery before any original work begins. This repo addresses that by automating the full lifecycle—from ideation through writeup—using a coordinated multiagent architecture, but it comes with operational trade‑offs that affect adoption in production settings.

What This Does
freephdlabor organizes work across 120+ files in freephdlabor/ and 63 files in externaltools/runexperimenttool/, encompassing agents for ideation, experimentation, review, and writeup. The system uses prompt files under freephdlabor/prompts/ to steer each agent, while toolkits in freephdlabor/toolkits/ provide concrete utilities such as arXiv fetching (freephdlabor/toolkits/generaltools/fetcharxivpapers/), file editing (freephdlabor/toolkits/generaltools/fileediting/), and knowledge‑base management (freephdlabor/toolkits/generaltools/kbrepomanagement/). A config file .llmconfig.yaml at the root lets you select models per component, and API keys are expected in .env. The framework supports two modes: running out‑of‑the‑box with python launchmultiagent.py --task "your idea", or customizing agents for domain‑specific problems by modifying or adding agents in freephdlabor/agents/.

How To Use It
Setup  
git clone https://github.com/ltjed/freephdlabor.git
cd freephdlabor
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate freephdlabor

Edit .env with your API keys (OPENAIAPIKEY, ANTHROPICAPIKEY, etc.) and optionally adjust model selection in .llmconfig.yaml.

Configuration  
Required environment variables are defined in .env; model preferences go in .llmconfig.yaml. No lockfile is present, so pip install -r externaltools/runexperimenttool/requirements.txt may pull incompatible versions across runs.

Running it  
python launchmultiagent.py --task "Your research idea or direction here"

The entry point launchmultiagent.py at the repo root orchestrates the agent workflow. For SLURM clusters, launchmultiagentslurm.sh is provided.

Real-World Use
A materials‑science team could fork the repo, define domain‑specific tools in freephdlabor/toolkits/ (e.g., a custom fetcharxivpapers filter for superconductor datasets), and add a new agent subclass in freephdlabor/agents/ to propose crystal‑structure hypotheses. The manager agent would then route ideation, experiment design, and writeup generation, producing a draft manuscript with figures and citations without manual copy‑pasting between tools.

Medium/SDLC - No CI/CD pipeline detected - no automated build/test gate - .github/ or CI config missing  
Low/Risk - Dependencies declared without a lockfile - non-reproducible builds - externaltools/runexperiment_tool/requirements.txt  
Low/Risk - Only 2 test files found; extensive agent logic lacks automated validation  

The repo includes a LICENSE file and basic documentation, but the absence of a lockfile and CI pipeline means builds are not fully reproducible and secret handling requires external processes.

The Bottom Line
This is a highly extensible multiagent framework that can automate end‑to‑end scientific workflows with minimal configuration, making it well‑suited for researchers who want to prototype or parallelize ideas across domains. However, the lack of a lockfile, CI/CD, and committed secrets in .env mean it demands disciplined operational practices—particularly around dependency management and credential hygiene—before it can be relied upon in production or shared collaboratively.

forks.name: Knowledge-Graph-Builder
forks.description: Repository for building knowledge graphs from specific datasets using generative language model through ollama
forks.summary:
The Problem

Extracting structured knowledge graphs from unstructured text typically requires either expensive commercial APIs or complex custom pipelines. Teams working with domain-specific documents (legal, technical, medical) need a way to produce source-grounded triples (head-relation-tail) using local or cloud LLMs, with the flexibility to swap backends and customize extraction prompts per domain.

What This Does

Knowledge Graph Builder (KGB) is a modular Python CLI for extracting, augmenting, and visualizing knowledge graphs from text. The pipeline runs four steps — extract triples, augment connectivity, convert to GraphML, and visualize — orchestrated through kgb/pipeline/runner.py and configured via YAML files in kgb/pipeline/configs/.

The client abstraction layer (kgb/clients/) supports three backends: Gemini API, Ollama, and LM Studio. Each has a provider implementation in kgb/clients/providers/ and a JSON config in kgb/clients/configs/. The domain system (kgb/domains/) ships with default and legal domains, each containing extraction prompts (promptopen.md, promptconstrained.md), augmentation strategies, and examples.

A notable feature is triple origin tracking: every extracted triple is tagged explicit, while augmented triples that bridge disconnected components are tagged contextual. The visualization step (kgb/visualization/graphviz.py) produces interactive Cytoscape.js HTML output with color-coded nodes by origin.

How To Use It

Setup: The project uses pyproject.toml with a Makefile wrapper. Run make install (auto-detects Python 3.11+) or manually create a venv and pip install -e ".[dev]".

Configuration: Required credentials vary by backend. Gemini needs GOOGLEAPIKEY in a .env file. Ollama requires a running local server (ollama serve). LM Studio needs its server enabled with a model loaded. No lockfile is present, so builds are not fully reproducible.

Running it: The entry point is kgb/main.py. Basic usage:

Interactive REPL
kgb

One-shot extraction
kgb extract --input data.jsonl --domain legal --client gemini

Full pipeline via YAML config
kgb run-pipeline --config kgb/pipeline/configs/legalollama.yaml

Full pipeline via flags
kgb run-pipeline --input data.jsonl --domain legal --client ollama \
  --extract --augment --convert --visualize

Individual steps work as documented: kgb augment connectivity, kgb convert, kgb visualize network, and kgb visualize extraction.

Real-World Use

A legal research team processing contracts could run the full pipeline against a JSONL corpus, producing a GraphML file for downstream graph analysis. The augmentation step bridges disconnected entities, making the resulting graph more useful for relationship discovery. The reports/triplequalityevaluation_gemma3.md suggests the authors already evaluated output quality with a local model. For teams with sensitive data, the Ollama/LM Studio backends keep everything on-premises.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No CI/CD pipeline: No .github/ or CI config exists. There's no automated build or test gate, so regressions can slip in.
Low - No dependency lockfile: pyproject.toml declares dependencies without a lockfile, making builds non-reproducible across environments.
Low - Only 3 test files: Tests exist but coverage is thin for a project with this many modules (40 Python files). The augmentation and visualization steps appear untested.
Low - Minimal documentation: Only 3 doc files and a README. The .claude/ and .agent/ skill files are agent-oriented, not user-facing docs.

The Bottom Line

KGB is a well-structured, genuinely useful tool for teams that need domain-customizable knowledge graph extraction with local LLM support. The multi-backend abstraction and origin tracking are thoughtful design choices. The main gaps are CI/CD and test coverage — acceptable for a research tool, but worth addressing before production use. Best suited for NLP engineers and data teams working with domain-specific corpora who want backend flexibility.

forks.name: FoodYou

The Problem  
Users who want a nutrition tracker without cloud sync or mandatory accounts have few Android options that keep all data on‑device and respect privacy. Existing solutions either rely on proprietary back‑ends or embed advertising, creating data‑leak risk.

What This Does  
FoodYou is an Android‑only app built with Kotlin Multiplatform (common + Android source sets). The core data model lives in app/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/maksimowiczm/foodyou/app/infrastructure/room/FoodYouDatabase.kt and is persisted locally via Room (FoodYouDatabase).  

The UI layers are modular:
 Home‑screen cards are defined in app/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/maksimowiczm/foodyou/app/ui/common/component/.kt.  
 Nutrition tracking, recipe creation and database imports live in the app/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/maksimowiczm/foodyou/app/ui/database/ packages.  

External food data is bundled as static JSON/CSV assets under app/src/commonMain/composeResources/files/, covering Open Food Facts, USDA and the Swiss Food Composition Database. Migration logic for schema changes is in app/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/maksimowiczm/foodyou/app/infrastructure/room/migration/.

How To Use It  

| Step | Evidence |
|------|----------|
| Clone & open | Repository root contains app/build.gradle.kts. |
| Install Android toolchain | Gradle wrapper (./gradlew) is present; no other build system is referenced. |

Real‑World Use  
A health‑tech startup could embed FoodYou as a “local‑only” mode in a broader wellness platform, letting users opt‑out of cloud sync. Integration point: launch FoodYouApplication (defined in app/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/maksimowiczm/foodyou/app/infrastructure/android/FoodYouApplication.kt) via an intent from the host app, then read the Room database (FoodYouDatabase) through the shared Koin module (RoomModule.android.kt).

val intent = Intent(context, FoodYouApplication::class.java)
context.startActivity(intent)

// Later, in host app:
val db = KoinJavaComponent.get(FoodYouDatabase::class.java)
val meals = db.mealDao().getAllMeals()

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Test coverage – Only 7 instrumented tests for migrations and crypto (app/src/androidInstrumentedTest/...). Core UI and business logic lack unit tests.  
Low – CI completeness – GitHub Actions run docs.yml, release-apk.yml, and validate-meals.yml; they do not run lint or static analysis on Kotlin code.  
Low – Dependency hygiene – build.gradle.kts does not lock versions via a versions.lock file; updating libraries requires manual review.
