forks.name: dmux
forks.description: A dev agent multiplexer for git worktrees and coding agents.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Running multiple AI coding agents on the same codebase causes file conflicts, branch collisions, and context pollution. Developers either serialize their agent work or risk agents overwriting each other's changes. There is no standard tool for orchestrating parallel agent sessions with proper git isolation.

What This Does

dmux is a tmux-based multiplexer that creates isolated git worktrees for each AI coding agent session. When you press n to create a new pane, it provisions a fresh worktree and branch, then launches your chosen agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, etc.) inside that pane. The tests/ directory contains 107 test files covering pane lifecycle, agent launch, git operations, and merge workflows.

The .dmux-hooks/ directory exposes lifecycle hooks (worktreecreated, premerge, post_merge) for custom scripting. The actions/ directory under tests/ shows the action system: merge, create PR, rename, duplicate, close, and toggle autopilot. The codebase is TypeScript (95 files) with React components (11 TSX files) for the UI layer.

Real-World Use

A team working on three features simultaneously runs dmux in their repo, creates three panes, and assigns each to a different agent. Agent A refactors the auth module in its worktree, Agent B adds a new API endpoint, Agent C fixes a bug. No agent sees the others' changes until each pane is merged via the menu (m → Merge). The team reviews each merge independently, avoiding the typical "merge hell" of parallel agent work.

Code Health & Issues

The repo appears well-structured with no obvious red flags. Evidence: 109 test files present, GitHub Actions CI configured in .github/workflows/publish.yml, MIT license included, and a lockfile present. However, the test count (109 files) against 95 TypeScript files suggests thorough coverage. The arnis-tile-cache/ directory (36 PNG files) is likely generated map tiles that should be in .gitignore — this adds ~1MB of binary artifacts to the repo. No secrets or config leaks detected.

The Bottom Line

dmux solves a real operational problem for teams running multiple AI coding agents. The worktree isolation pattern is sound, and the hook system allows integration into existing workflows. Best suited for teams that already use tmux and want to parallelize agent work without collisions. Solo developers may find the tmux dependency heavy — a terminal multiplexer on top of a multiplexer adds complexity that a simpler CLI might avoid.

forks.name: agent-flow
forks.description: Real-time visualization of Claude Code agent orchestration — see your agents think, branch, and coordinate as they work.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Claude Code and Codex execute agentic workflows as black boxes. You see inputs and final outputs, but the intermediate reasoning, tool call chains, and subagent coordination remain invisible. Debugging failures means guessing at what happened inside the agent loop.

What This Does

Agent Flow captures real-time events from Claude Code and Codex sessions and renders them as an interactive node graph on an HTML canvas. The extension/src/ directory contains watchers for both runtimes: session-watcher.ts monitors Claude Code's project files, while codex-session-watcher.ts tails Codex's JSONL rollout files. Events flow through a relay server (scripts/relay.ts) to the web frontend.

The web UI in web/components/agent-visualizer/ renders agents as nodes with animated tool calls, edges for branching/return flows, and panels for timelines, transcripts, and file attention heatmaps. The canvas renderer (canvas/draw-agents.ts, canvas/draw-edges.ts) handles pan/zoom and hit detection for clicking into details.

Real-World Use

Run npx agent-flow-app in one terminal, start a Claude Code session in another. Watch agents spawn subagents, make tool calls (edit files, run commands), and return results—all visualized in real time. When a build fails, trace the exact tool call sequence that led there instead of re-running with verbose logging.

Low – No CI/CD pipeline in .github/. No automated build or test gate, despite 8 test files present. Risk of regressions on merge.
Medium – scripts/telemetry/ directory sends usage data. The sanitize.ts file suggests PII scrubbing, but telemetry is opt-out (no consent prompt visible in the README setup flow).

Low – 8 test files exist (extension/test/, scripts/telemetry.test.ts) but coverage is sparse relative to 84 TypeScript files. Core watchers (session-watcher.ts, codex-session-watcher.ts) lack tests.

The Bottom Line

Agent Flow solves a real debugging pain point for anyone building multi-step agent workflows with Claude Code or Codex. The architecture is clean—separate watchers, a relay server, and a canvas-based UI—and it works out of the box with npx agent-flow-app. It's most valuable for teams shipping agent-heavy features who need observability into agent behavior. FckSignups is a curated directory of open-source, in-browser tools that require no signup. The frontend is a React + TypeScript single-page app (src/App.tsx) that renders a searchable, filterable grid of tools. Data lives in tools.json, which the app loads via the useTools hook (src/hooks/useTools.ts). Each tool entry follows a defined schema (src/types/index.ts) with fields like id, name, description, url, category, and optional tags, github, license, and stars.

The UI is componentized: ToolGrid renders cards, Controls handles search/filter, and SubmitToolModal lets users propose new tools. A cloudflare-worker/worker.ts exists as a serverless backend, likely for fetching GitHub star counts dynamically. A Python script (managementtools/addTool.py) automates adding new tools to tools.json.

How To Use It

Setup and running — the README documents the full flow:

git clone https://github.com/BraveOPotato/FckSignups.git && \
cd FckSignups && \
npm install && \
npm run dev

This starts the Vite dev server (vite.config.ts). There are no environment variables or API keys needed for local development. For the Cloudflare Worker, you'd need a Cloudflare account and wrangler configured (cloudflare-worker/wrangler.toml exists), but the core app runs standalone.

Real-World Use

A developer needing a quick QR code generator, JSON formatter, or image resizer can open the site, search by category or keyword, and click straight through to a working tool. The directory serves as a front-door aggregator — a "bookmark manager" for no-signup utilities. Medium - No CI/CD pipeline — .github/ contains only an issue template, no workflows. No automated build or lint gate on commits.

The codebase is small and organized with clear separation of concerns (components, hooks, constants, types). The Cloudflare Worker is a sensible addition for live star counts, but it adds deployment complexity for a static directory.

The Bottom Line

FckSignups is a clean, well-structured directory app that solves a real friction point. It's simple to run locally and easy to extend via tools.json. The lack of tests and CI is acceptable for a community-curated list but would need addressing if this were to become a production service. forks.name: DeepCAD
forks.description: code for our ICCV 2021 paper "DeepCAD: A Deep Generative Network for Computer-Aided Design Models"
forks.summary:
The Problem

Generating 3D CAD models programmatically is difficult because most deep generative models operate on meshes or voxels, not on the construction sequences that CAD software actually uses. Engineers need a way to generate valid, editable CAD models that preserve the original design intent—not just shape approximations.

What This Does

DeepCAD is an ICCV 2021 paper implementation that learns to generate CAD models as construction sequences. The pipeline uses a two-stage approach: an autoencoder (model/autoencoder.py) compresses CAD sequences into a latent space, then a latent GAN (model/latentGAN.py) generates novel sequences from random noise. The vectorized representation is defined in cadlib/macro.py and handles the core CAD operations—extrusions, sketches, and boolean operations.

Data flows from Onshape JSON files through dataset/json2vec.py for training, and results export to STEP format via utils/export2step.py. The trainer/ directory separates training logic for the autoencoder (trainerAE.py) and the latent GAN (trainerLGAN.py), with loss functions in trainer/loss.py.

Real-World Use

A mechanical design team could train DeepCAD on their library of existing CAD models, then use the trained generator to produce novel part variations for concept exploration. The output is a construction sequence, not a mesh, so engineers can open the result in Onshape or SolidWorks and edit parameters directly.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No CI/CD pipeline - No .github/ or CI config detected. No automated test gate for pull requests.
Low - Non-reproducible builds - requirements.txt without lockfile means dependency versions may drift across environments.
Low - Single test file - Only 1 test file found (test.py), which appears to be a runtime test script, not unit tests. Coverage is minimal.
Med - External dependency risk - Requires pythonocc-core via conda, which is version-sensitive and platform-dependent (Linux only per README).

The Bottom Line

DeepCAD is a well-structured research codebase that solves a real problem—generating CAD construction sequences rather than meshes. The autoencoder + latent GAN architecture is cleanly separated, and the evaluation scripts (evaluation/) provide meaningful metrics (Chamfer distance, command accuracy). It is suitable for researchers or teams who need to extend generative CAD work, but the lack of tests and CI makes it risky as a production dependency without significant hardening.

What This Does

Ponytail is a prompt-layer plugin that installs a decision hierarchy into AI agents across 10 platforms (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, OpenCode, and others via hooks/ and skills/ directories). Before generating code, the agent checks a 6-step ladder: does the feature need to exist at all, does the standard library handle it, is there a native platform feature, is an installed dependency sufficient, can it be one line, and only then—write the minimum viable code.

The hooks/ directory contains lifecycle scripts (ponytail-activate.js, ponytail-config.js, ponytail-instructions.js) that inject this ruleset at session start. The skills/ directory provides three skill levels (ponytail, ponytail-review, ponytail-help), and commands/ maps agent commands like /ponytail ultra to specific behaviors. The pi-extension/ folder is a VS Code extension harness.

Real-World Use

A developer asks an agent for an email validation function. Without Ponytail, the agent writes a regex, imports a validation library, and adds test scaffolding. With Ponytail, the agent outputs:

The ponytail: comment marks the shortcut and names the upgrade path if requirements change. The benchmarks/ directory contains reproducible test harnesses across three models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) showing 80-94% less code, 47-77% lower cost, and 3-6x faster generation versus a baseline agent.

Code Health & Issues
Medium/SDLC - No CI/CD pipeline - No workflow files in .github/, no build or test gate. Changes are not automatically validated, which is a gap for team adoption.
Low/Risk - No lockfile - package.json exists without package-lock.json or yarn.lock. Dependencies are non-reproducible across environments.
Low/Risk - Heuristic-only benchmarks - The benchmarks/ directory uses promptfoo and reports median results, but the sample size (10 runs per cell) is modest. Results are directional, not statistically rigorous.

The codebase is well-organized, with clear separation between platform-specific plugins (pi-extension/, .opencode/, .cursor/) and shared logic (hooks/, skills/). The absence of CI is the most material gap.

The Bottom Line

Ponytail solves a real and costly problem—agent over-generation—with a clever, lightweight approach that works across major AI coding tools. The benchmark results are compelling, and the decision hierarchy is well-reasoned. It's best suited for teams that want to cut agent costs and code volume, but the lack of CI and lockfile means it's more of a productivity tool than a production dependency. Worth installing for any team using AI coding agents regularly.

forks.name: dgl
forks.description: Python package built to ease deep learning on graph, on top of existing DL frameworks.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Building and training graph neural networks (GNNs) requires handling irregular graph structures efficiently, especially on GPUs. Existing deep learning frameworks lack native support for graph operations, forcing developers to implement custom message passing, neighbor sampling, and sparse matrix kernels. This creates significant engineering overhead and performance bottlenecks.

What Does

DGL provides a graph object that lives on CPU or GPU, bundling structural data with node/edge features. The dglsparse/ directory contains C++/CUDA kernels for sparse matrix operations (SPMM, SDDMM, edge softmax) that form the backbone of GNN message passing. The dglgo/ package offers a CLI (dglgo/dglgo/cli/cli.py) for training and applying pre-built pipelines, with Jinja templates for node prediction, graph prediction, and link prediction tasks.

The repo includes benchmark suites under benchmarks/benchmarks/ covering API performance (neighbor sampling, graph construction), kernel performance (gspmm, gsddmm), and model accuracy/speed for architectures like GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, and RGCN. These use ASV (airspeed velocity) for tracking performance regressions.

Real-World Use

A team building a recommendation system on a user-item interaction graph could use DGL's neighbor sampling (benchfusedsampleneighbors.py) to train a GraphSAGE model on a billion-edge graph distributed across GPUs. The workflow: load graph data into a DGL graph object, define a GraphSAGE model using dglgo/dglgo/model/nodeencoder/sage.py, and run distributed training with the multi-GPU benchmarks as reference.

Code Health & Issues
Low - Minimal test coverage. Only 2 test files found for a 200-file repo. Core functionality in dglsparse/src/ and the dglgo pipeline code lacks unit tests. This increases risk of regressions.
Low - Build complexity. The project uses CMake, conda packaging, and Jenkins CI. The CMakeLists.txt and conda/dgl/meta.yaml suggest a non-trivial build pipeline that may be difficult to reproduce locally.
Low - Dependency on external frameworks. DGL must stay synchronized with PyTorch, TensorFlow, and MXNet APIs. The repo does not show version pinning for these dependencies, which could cause breakage on upgrades.

The repo is structurally sound: CI is configured (Jenkinsfile, .github/workflows/lint.yml), a license is present, and benchmarks are well-organized. The sparse kernel implementations in dgl_sparse/src/ appear production-grade with separate CPU/GPU paths.

The Bottom Line

DGL is the most mature Python framework for GNNs, with proven performance at scale and broad model coverage. The sparse kernel library and distributed training support are genuinely production-ready. The main risk is the thin test coverage, which makes it better suited for teams that can invest in their own validation rather than teams needing a drop-in solution. Setup  
Install Go (>=1.22) then fetch dependencies
go mod tidy

Build the server binary
go build -o cyberstrike-server ./cmd/server

Build the MCP stdio client (optional)
go build -o mcp-stdio ./cmd/mcp-stdio

Edit config.yaml (present at the repo root) to set server ports, TLS certificates, and AI model endpoints. The file is parsed by internal/config/config.go. Example keys include server.port, tls.certpath, and ai.provider. No environment‑variable overrides are defined in the code base.

Start the web console and C2 services
./cyberstrike-server -config ./config.yaml

The server listens on the port defined in config.yaml and serves the UI assets bundled in images/. For command‑line interaction use the MCP client:

./mcp-stdio -mode stdio   # talks to the running server via the native MCP protocol

The repository also contains test harnesses (cmd/test-config/main.go, cmd/test-external-mcp/main.go) that can be executed to validate configuration and MCP connectivity.

engage.Start()

The platform automatically runs the selected security tools, records each step in the audit log (internal/audit/), and indexes findings into the SQLite knowledge base (internal/knowledge/einosqliteindexer.go). forks.name: dnsfs
forks.description: Store your data in others DNS resolver cache
forks.summary:
The Problem

Standard cloud storage costs money per gigabyte. DNS caches are free, globally distributed, and have no per-byte billing. This project exploits that infrastructure by encoding file data into DNS queries that get cached by recursive resolvers worldwide, creating a read-only filesystem with zero hosting cost.

What This Does

dnsfs is a Go-based FUSE filesystem that stores and retrieves data through DNS resolver caches. The core logic in dnsfs/dns.go handles encoding file blocks into DNS TXT record queries, while dnsfs/http.go serves an HTTP interface for Prometheus metrics and health checks. The dnsfs/main.go entry point wires together the FUSE mount, DNS query engine, and HTTP server.

Data is split into chunks, each chunk gets a unique subdomain under a domain you control. When a recursive resolver caches the TXT response, that chunk becomes accessible globally until the TTL expires. The bulk-mmlookup/main.go tool performs mass geolocation lookups against MaxMind GeoIP2 data to measure which resolvers have cached your data. retention-check/main.go and retention-stats/main.go analyze how long data persists in various resolver caches.

Real-World Use

Deploy a DNS server authoritatively serving your domain, run dnsfs to write a file, then query chunk123.yourdomain.com from any DNS resolver worldwide. The resolver caches the TXT record, and the file chunk is retrievable until the TTL expires. Useful for ephemeral file distribution to regions with restricted internet access, where DNS is often the only unblocked protocol.

Code Health & Issues
High - No test files - Zero test coverage across all four entry points (dnsfs/main.go, bulk-mmlookup/main.go, retention-check/main.go, retention-stats/main.go). The DNS query logic in dnsfs/dns.go and HTTP server in dnsfs/http.go have no unit or integration tests. This is a significant risk for a project that interacts with real network infrastructure.

Low - Vendor directory bloat - 188 files in vendor/ (94% of repository) with vendored dependencies including Prometheus, protobuf, and MaxMind GeoIP libraries. Standard Go modules would be cleaner.

The Bottom Line

dnsfs is a clever proof-of-concept demonstrating DNS cache exploitation for file storage. The core idea is interesting for security research and censorship circumvention, but the complete absence of tests, CI, and licensing makes it unsuitable for production use or as a dependency. Use it as a reference implementation for understanding DNS caching mechanics, not as a deployable filesystem.

forks.name: agent-device
forks.description: CLI to control iOS and Android devices for AI agents
forks.summary:
Controlling mobile devices with precision from the command line has long been a challenge for developers and researchers building AI agents that interact with real-world apps. Most existing solutions are either platform-specific, rely on clunky GUIs, or demand heavy dependencies and complex setups. Imagine you’re developing an AI agent that needs to navigate a mobile app, trigger alerts, or capture screenshots — all without manual intervention or fragile scripting. This is the gap agent-device aims to bridge: providing seamless, low-dependency device automation for both iOS and Android, directly from the CLI, as a foundation for higher-level agent workflows.

Agent-device distinguishes itself by focusing on minimalism and universality. Inspired by Vercel’s agent-browser, but tailored for mobile platforms, this project exposes a unified command suite covering both iOS and Android, with direct Node.js execution — no transpilation or build step required. The commands are ergonomically designed: you can open apps, simulate interactions like presses or typing, inspect UI accessibility trees, and even manipulate device settings like Wi-Fi or airplane mode. What’s compelling is the deliberate avoidance of heavy frameworks; everything is driven via platform tooling like adb for Android and simctl/devicectl for iOS, with rich snapshot and inspection features that are usually missing from open-source mobile automation tools.

Architecturally, agent-device leverages a hybrid approach to device interaction, evident from its file structure. The CLI entrypoint, bin/agent-device.mjs, is written in TypeScript and executed directly on Node 22+, which is a strategic choice for speed and maintainability. On the iOS side, you’ll find a native Swift runner (ios-runner/AgentDeviceRunner) and an AXSnapshot module — the latter exposing accessibility tree snapshots via AX and XCTest backends. The hybrid snapshot logic described in the README is implemented by first querying AX (fast but sometimes incomplete) and then supplementing with scoped XCTest queries, yielding a more reliable UI tree. The iOS runner is built as an Xcode project, including test suites (AgentDeviceRunnerUITests/RunnerTests.swift) and asset catalogs; this modularity allows for easy extension and debugging, a design pattern rarely seen in cross-platform CLI tools. Meanwhile, Android interactions are orchestrated via adb, with all device commands abstracted behind the CLI. The documentation (docs/ios-automation.md, docs/ios-runner-protocol.md) clarifies the protocol and integration points, which will be useful for contributors or those extending the tool.

Developers working on AI agents that need to interact with real devices (or simulators/emulators) will immediately see the value in agent-device. For instance, you might be building a reinforcement learning agent that adapts its strategy based on app state — the snapshot command gives you a stable, semantic map of the UI, and actions like click or type can be targeted by accessibility refs rather than brittle coordinates. Another scenario: automated regression testing workflows can use agent-device to script end-to-end flows across both Android and iOS, including capturing screenshots or toggling settings, all from a single CLI. And for those prototyping new app features, the ability to quickly open, interact, and inspect apps in diverse device contexts — without wrestling with Appium or platform-specific wrappers — is a productivity boon.

The significance of agent-device goes beyond convenience; it’s about enabling robust, agent-driven automation for mobile apps, lowering the barrier to experimentation, and facilitating reproducible interactions. The project’s modular architecture, minimalist dependency footprint, and thoughtful abstraction of platform quirks signal a new direction for open-source device tooling. As AI agents increasingly move from browser automation to mobile, having a reliable, scriptable bridge is crucial — and agent-device, even in its experimental stage, is poised to become a foundational piece in this ecosystem. Developers seeking to automate, test, or research mobile UI flows should keep a close eye on its evolution.

forks.name: fastapi-voyager
forks.description: Visualize your API endpoints and explore them interactively, also support Django ninja & Litestar
forks.summary:
The Problem

Ever felt like you're spelunking through someone else's API just to figure out what routes exist and where they lead? Sure, Swagger UI helps, but it’s a glorified list of endpoints—zero context about how your code modules are organized. If you’re working on a FastAPI, Django Ninja, or Litestar project, you probably want more than just "here’s a GET endpoint." You want a bird’s-eye view of your API structure, tied to the actual code, not just the HTTP layer. Enter fastapi-voyager.

What This Does

fastapi-voyager gives you an interactive visualization of your API endpoints, mapped to modules in your codebase. It’s not just for FastAPI—it also supports Django Ninja and Litestar. The heavy lifting happens in src/fastapivoyager/adapters/, with framework-specific adapters like djangoninjaadapter.py and fastapiadapter.py. The core functionality is exposed through the createvoyager function in src/fastapivoyager/init.py. 

You mount the Voyager UI as a sub-application (e.g., /voyager), and it shows you all your endpoints, module color-coding, and even links back to your repo for source browsing. If you’re feeling fancy, you can configure options like modulecolor to differentiate code modules visually, or swaggerurl for quick access to your Swagger docs. The CLI (src/fastapivoyager/cli.py) also lets you spin up Voyager without embedding it into a larger application—perfect for debugging.

Real-World Use

Let’s say you’ve inherited a sprawling FastAPI app with routes scattered across multiple modules. First, install fastapi-voyager:

pip install fastapi-voyager

Add Voyager to your app:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapivoyager import createvoyager

app = FastAPI()

app.mount('/voyager', createvoyager(app, module_color={'src.services': 'tomato'}))

Run your app, and hit http://localhost:8000/voyager. Now, you’ve got a visual map of your endpoints, organized by code module. Bonus: link it to your repo URL and click directly into the source code for each route. For Django Ninja or Litestar, the setup is similar—just swap the adapter.

The Bottom Line

If you’re working on mid-to-large projects with messy endpoint sprawl, fastapi-voyager is worth a look. It’s not perfect—sub-applications are unsupported, and it feels very early-stage (Pydantic v2-only, no stars yet). But for dev teams needing better API clarity, it’s a solid documentation tool. For solo devs on small projects? Probably overkill.

forks.name: RapidRAW
forks.description: A beautiful, non-destructive, and GPU-accelerated RAW image editor built with performance in mind.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Processing high-resolution RAW photos is computationally expensive. Existing tools like Adobe Lightroom are resource-heavy and slow, while open-source alternatives often lack GPU acceleration or modern UI design. Photographers need a fast, non-destructive editor that runs on modest hardware without compromising image quality.

What This Does

RapidRAW is a cross-platform RAW image editor built on Tauri, React, and WebGPU (via wgpu). The Rust backend in src-tauri/src/adjustmentutils.rs and src-tauri/src/aicommands.rs handles computationally intensive tasks like demosaicing and lens correction. The lens correction database lives in src-tauri/lensfundb/, with per-manufacturer XML files (e.g., slr-canon.xml, mil-sony.xml). GPU acceleration runs through wgpu shaders, enabling real-time preview of adjustments like exposure, white balance, and tone curves.

The frontend uses React with TypeScript, communicating with the Rust backend via Tauri's IPC layer. The project bundles Android support through src-tauri/gen/android/, with Gradle build scripts and Kotlin integration in src-tauri/src/androidintegration.rs. CI/CD pipelines in .github/workflows/ build and test across Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android.

Real-World Use

A photographer imports a folder of 50MP RAW files from a Canon R5. RapidRAW reads the embedded JPEG preview for instant thumbnail display, then processes the full RAW data on the GPU. The user adjusts exposure and white balance in real-time—each slider move triggers a WGSL compute shader that updates the preview in milliseconds. All edits remain non-destructive, stored as a sidecar file or embedded metadata.

Code Health & Issues
High - No test files detected - The repository contains zero test files across Rust, TypeScript, or Kotlin code. Image processing pipelines are notoriously error-prone (edge cases in demosaicing, lens correction, color space conversion). Untested code paths will produce hard-to-diagnose artifacts.
Medium - No input validation visible - RAW parsers and lens correction databases accept external data (camera metadata, lens profiles). Missing validation in src-tauri/src/adjustment_utils.rs could lead to crashes or undefined behavior on malformed input.
Medium - Dependency management risk - The project depends on wgpu, Tauri, and Rust crates for GPU compute. Version pinning in Cargo.toml and package.json is unclear; breaking changes in GPU APIs could silently corrupt output.
Low - No linting or formatting CI for Rust - CI workflows in .github/workflows/ run lint checks for JavaScript/TypeScript but omit cargo clippy or rustfmt. Code consistency relies on developer discipline.

The Bottom Line

RapidRAW is an ambitious project that successfully combines modern web tech with native GPU compute for RAW processing. The architecture is sound—Tauri for cross-platform packaging, wgpu for GPU acceleration, React for UI. The lack of tests and input validation makes it risky for production use today. It's best suited for photographers comfortable with beta software who want to experiment with GPU-accelerated editing on Linux or Android, where mature alternatives are scarce.

forks.name: pyvideotrans
forks.description: Translate the video from one language to another and embed dubbing & subtitles.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Translating video content between languages typically requires multiple disjointed tools for speech recognition, translation, and dubbing. Teams waste time stitching together separate ASR, machine translation, and TTS pipelines, then manually syncing audio with video. This repo provides a single, integrated workflow for the entire pipeline.

What This Does

pyVideoTrans is a desktop application and CLI tool that takes a video in one language and produces a dubbed, subtitled version in another. The core pipeline lives in videotrans/task/job.py and videotrans/task/onlyone.py—these orchestrate the three-stage process: ASR (speech-to-text), translation, and TTS (text-to-speech). Each stage supports multiple backends. For recognition, videotrans/recognition/ contains 20+ modules including local Whisper (whisper.py), cloud APIs (google.py, azure.py), and specialized models (funasr.py). Translation is handled by videotrans/translator/ with 25+ providers from DeepSeek (deepseek.py) to local models (localllm.py). TTS backends in videotrans/tts/ range from free Edge-TTS (edgetts.py) to voice cloning via F5-TTS (f5tts.py) and CosyVoice (cosyvoice.py).

The CLI entry point is cli.py. The GUI is built with PyQt5 in videotrans/mainwin/mainwin.py. Configuration lives in videotrans/configure/. The app supports interactive editing at each pipeline stage—users can pause and correct recognition or translation before proceeding.

Real-World Use

A content creator records a tutorial in English and needs a Spanish version. They configure the app to use Faster-Whisper for recognition, DeepSeek for translation, and Edge-TTS for Spanish dubbing. The pipeline runs automatically: the app extracts audio, transcribes it to SRT (videotrans/task/speech2text.py), translates the SRT (videotrans/task/translatesrt.py), generates dubbed audio with speaker diarization support (videotrans/recognition/stt.py handles speaker labels), and remuxes the final video. The user can review and edit the translated subtitles before dubbing via the interactive UI.

Code Health & Issues

The Bottom Line

pyVideoTrans is a genuinely useful integration tool that solves a real multi-step workflow problem. The codebase is functional but unpolished—thin tests, potential duplication, and no reproducible builds. Teams needing a quick video translation pipeline should evaluate it, but production deployments will require hardening the dependency management and adding test coverage for their chosen providers.

forks.name: PersonaLive
forks.description: [CVPR 2026] PersonaLive! : Expressive Portrait Image Animation for Live Streaming
forks.summary:
The Problem

PersonaLive addresses the challenge of real-time, expressive portrait image animation for live streaming. Existing diffusion-based animation models are typically too slow for interactive use or produce degraded results over long sessions. PersonaLive targets infinite-length, streamable animation with a single reference portrait image and a driving video source, aiming to maintain identity fidelity and expression quality without latency buildup.

What This Does

PersonaLive is a diffusion-based framework that animates a static portrait image using motion cues from a driving video. The core pipeline is split into three stages (configs/train/personalivestage1.yaml, stage2, stage3), each handling a distinct part of the generation process—likely coarse motion, fine detail, and temporal consistency. The src/ directory contains the full model stack: U-Net variants (src/models/unet2dcondition.py, unet3d.py), motion encoders, pose guiders, and StyleGAN2 discriminators for training.

The repo ships three inference paths: a standard offline script (inferenceoffline.py), a streaming variant (inferenceonline.py), and a real-time webcam pipeline under webcam/. The webcam frontend is a SvelteKit app with TypeScript (webcam/frontend/src/lib/index.ts), providing a browser-based UI for controlling the animation pipeline. TensorRT and ONNX export support exists via src/modeling/onnxexport.py and torch2trt.py for optimized deployment.

How To Use It

Setup: Install Python dependencies with pip install -r requirementsbase.txt (training requires requirementstrain.txt). The webcam frontend uses npm—run npm install inside webcam/frontend/.

Configuration: Model weights go in pretrainedweights/ (download via python tools/downloadweights.py). Inference parameters are set in the YAML files under configs/inference/ (e.g., inferencestage1&2.yaml). The webcam backend reads webcam/config.py for runtime settings.

Running it: For offline animation, run inferenceoffline.py with a reference image and driving video. For the webcam interface, start the backend and Svelte frontend:

Offline inference
python inferenceoffline.py --config configs/inference/inferencestage1&2.yaml

Webcam backend (Svelte frontend served via vite)
cd webcam/frontend && npm run dev

Training scripts are trainstage1.py, trainstage2.py, trainstage3.py.

Real-World Use

A live-streaming platform could deploy PersonaLive to let creators animate a custom avatar from their webcam feed. The webcam pipeline (webcam/vid2vid.py) takes the user's camera stream, extracts motion, and drives the reference portrait in near real-time. For production, the TensorRT path (webcam/vid2vidtrt.py) would be used to hit latency targets on GPU servers. The streaming strategy in inferenceonline.py is designed to run on 12GB VRAM, making it feasible on mid-range GPUs.

Code Health & Issues
High - No test files detected - The entire repo lacks a test suite. Given the complexity of the diffusion pipeline and webcam streaming, untested code paths are a significant risk for regressions.
High - No CI/CD pipeline - No .github/ workflows or CI config exist. There is no automated gate for build or test validation.
Med - Training reproducibility - The three-stage training setup requires careful configuration and pretrained base models (sd-image-variations-diffusers, sd-vae-ft-mse). Without a documented training walkthrough or logs, reproducing results will be difficult.
Med - Dependency hygiene - Multiple requirement files (requirementsbase.txt, requirementstrain.txt, requirements_trt.txt) suggest a complex dependency matrix. The C++/CUDA files under src/stylegan2/ require a compatible build environment.
Low - Documentation gaps - The README covers installation and inference but lacks detailed docs for the webcam pipeline setup, TensorRT conversion, and training data preparation.

The Bottom Line

PersonaLive is a serious research implementation with a clear architecture and working inference paths. The webcam frontend and TensorRT support indicate real deployment intent, not just paper code. It is best suited for researchers and engineers who need a working portrait animation baseline and are comfortable debugging a research-grade codebase without tests or CI. Production teams should budget time for hardening before relying on it.

forks.summary:
The Problem

Operating a regulated sportsbook across Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana means dealing with three different payment rails (M-Pesa, Flutterwave), three tax regimes, and a national gambling license requirement (BCLB in Kenya) that mandates KYC, geolocation, and responsible-gaming controls. Most open-source betting platforms are single-country, single-payment, and ignore compliance entirely. lets-bet attempts to solve the multi-tenant compliance and payments problem in one codebase.

What This Does

lets-bet is a Go microservices platform for sports betting and crash games (Aviator-style), built around a multi-tenant architecture where country-specific logic lives in internal/tenant/ (ke/ for M-Pesa and BCLB tax, ng/ and gh/ for Flutterwave). The core betting engine in internal/core/usecase/ handles bet placement, wallet transactions with optimistic locking, and a provably-fair crash game algorithm. Real-time odds and game state flow over WebSockets via internal/infrastructure/websocket/hub.go.

The platform runs five services (cmd/gateway, cmd/wallet, cmd/engine, cmd/settlement, cmd/games) communicating over NATS with PostgreSQL persistence and Redis caching. Compliance features are substantial: Smile ID KYC, MaxMind geolocation, tax calculation, and a full internal/compliance/bclb/ module for Kenyan regulatory reporting. The internal/security/ directory includes GDPR, responsible gaming, and penetration-testing assessment services.

How To Use It

The repo includes a Makefile, docker-compose.yml, and a multi-service deployments/docker/Dockerfile, so local development runs through Docker.

Setup:
git clone <repo-url>
cd lets-bet
cp .env.example .env
docker-compose up -d

Configuration: Copy .env.example to .env and populate credentials for M-Pesa (Daraja API keys), Flutterwave, Smile ID, MaxMind GeoLite2, PostgreSQL, Redis, and NATS. Country-specific payment adapters in internal/tenant/ read these settings.

Running: After docker-compose up, the API gateway listens on port 8080. Database migrations run via cmd/migrate/main.go. The Makefile provides targets for build, test, and lint. Load testing uses k6 scripts in loadtests/k6/.

Real-World Use

A Kenyan operator would run the gateway, wallet, engine, settlement, and games services behind Cloudflare. A user places a bet, the engine validates it, applies 15% GGR tax via internal/core/usecase/tax/tax.go, reserves funds atomically in the wallet service, and publishes a NATS event. The settlement service consumes the event, determines the outcome, and triggers an M-Pesa payout via internal/tenant/ke/mpesa.go. BCLB reporting runs in internal/compliance/bclb/reporting.go.

Code Health & Issues
High – Security assessment modules (internal/security/pentest/, internal/security/audit/) appear to be in-repo penetration testing and audit tooling. Running these against production is risky; their presence suggests either a novel compliance feature or scope creep.
Medium – No migration files visible in the structure despite cmd/migrate/main.go and a migrations/ folder mentioned in the README. Schema management is unclear.

The Bottom Line

lets-bet is a serious, well-architected attempt at a genuinely hard problem: multi-country betting with real compliance. The tenant adapter pattern and event-driven core are sound. It is not production-ready without adding payment-rail tests and clarifying migrations, but as a reference architecture for regulated betting platforms, it is unusually complete. forks.summary:
The Problem  
Teams building agentic applications often lack a reusable, provider‑agnostic “skill” that encodes disciplined harness design (validation, authorization, observation logging, etc.). Without a shared reference, each project reinvents the same patterns, leading to inconsistent security, poor observability, and higher maintenance cost.

What This Does  
agents-best-practices ships a provider‑neutral Agent Skill that can be added to any Codex or Claude Code agent via the skills framework. The core artifact is SKILL.md, which defines the skill’s interface, runtime expectations, and example prompts. Supporting markdown files in references/ (e.g., architecture.md, mvp-agent-blueprint.md, security-evals-observability.md) provide detailed design checklists, loop diagrams, and audit guidelines that agents can surface on demand.

 README.md – overview, badge links, and three installation pathways.  
 SKILL.md – formal skill description consumed by the skills runtime.  
 references/.md – concrete content the skill can render (blueprints, checklists, prompts).  

Because the repository contains only documentation, the skill itself is data‑driven; the consuming agent runtime supplies the execution logic.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Global install via the skills CLI (recommended for any project):  

   npx skills add DenisSergeevitch/agents-best-practices -g
Manual clone (if the CLI is unavailable). Choose the appropriate provider directory and run the command from the README:  

   # Example for Claude Code, user‑level
   mkdir -p "$HOME/.claude/skills"
   git clone https://github.com/DenisSergeevitch/agents-best-practices.git \
     "$HOME/.claude/skills/agents-best-practices"

   The clone creates the expected layout (SKILL.md, icon.jpeg, references/).

Configuration  
No additional configuration files are shipped. The consuming agent must point its skill loader to the installed directory (the skills runtime resolves this automatically). If a project needs custom prompts or overrides, it can edit the markdown files directly—there is no code‑level config to modify.

Running It  
After installation, invoke the skill from any conversation that mentions agent architecture, tool permissions, planning, or related topics. The skills runtime will:
Detect the trigger phrase (e.g., “generate an MVP agent blueprint”).  
Load the corresponding markdown file from references/ (e.g., mvp-agent-blueprint.md).  
Return the formatted guidance to the user or to downstream tool calls.

No executable entry point exists in the repo; the skill’s behavior is entirely driven by the host agent’s runtime.

Real‑World Use  
A fintech firm deploying a compliance‑monitoring agent can add this skill to its Claude Code instance. When a developer asks, “What safety checks should I add before sending customer data to an external API?”, the skill pulls references/security-evals-observability.md and returns a checklist of validation, permission gating, and audit‑log requirements that the developer can embed directly into the agent’s harness.

User > How do I safely call the external credit‑score API?
Agent > Load security checklist from agents-best-practices:
Validate input schema…
Verify permission readprivatedata…
Record request/response in audit log…

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No executable code – the repo consists solely of markdown; any runtime bugs will surface only in the consuming agent, not in this repo.  
Medium – No automated tests – no .test. files or test framework configuration; validation of skill content relies on manual review.  
Medium – No CI/CD pipeline – absence of .github/workflows or similar means no gate for linting or link‑checking.  
Low – License present – LICENSE provides MIT terms, satisfying legal reuse.  
Low – Documentation completeness – README.md and SKILL.md clearly describe installation; however, there is no versioning or changelog to track updates.

The Bottom Line  
agents-best-practices delivers a well‑structured, provider‑agnostic knowledge base that can be plugged into any Codex or Claude Code agent via the skills framework. It excels as a reference library for harness design and audit checklists, but it provides no code to test or execute directly. Teams that already use the skills runtime will find immediate value; organizations without that infrastructure will need to adopt the runtime first. Absence of tests and CI means the repository’s quality rests on manual maintenance.

forks.name: optuna
forks.description: A hyperparameter optimization framework
forks.summary:
The Problem

Hyperparameter optimization in machine learning is often handled with rigid, static search spaces that require boilerplate configuration files. Popular libraries like GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV lack support for dynamic search spaces, efficient pruning of unpromising trials, and distributed execution without significant code restructuring.

What This Does

Optuna is a Python framework for automated hyperparameter optimization. The core API in optuna/cli.py and optuna/init.py implements a define-by-run pattern where search spaces are constructed imperatively inside an objective function using trial.suggestfloat(), trial.suggestint(), and trial.suggestcategorical() calls. The optuna/samplers/ directory contains 12 sampling algorithms including TPE (tpe/sampler.py), CMA-ES (cmaes.py), and NSGA-II/III for multi-objective optimization. The optuna/pruners/ directory provides early-stopping strategies like Hyperband (hyperband.py) and Median pruner (median.py) that terminate low-performing trials automatically.

The visualization module in docs/visualizationexamples/ generates optimization history plots, parallel coordinate charts, and parameter importance rankings. Integration modules in optuna/integration/ support LightGBM, XGBoost, PyTorch Lightning, TensorFlow, and 15 other ML frameworks.

Real-World Use

A team training a neural network on image classification can define a search space with 8-12 hyperparameters (learning rate, layer sizes, dropout rates) and run 500 trials across 4 machines. The TPE sampler learns from completed trials to focus on promising regions, while the Median pruner stops trials that underperform after 20% of epochs. Results are stored in a SQLite or MySQL database via optuna/storages/.

Code Health & Issues

The codebase is well-maintained with no structural red flags. Key observations:
Low - Missing integration tests for artifact storage backends (optuna/artifacts/boto3.py, gcs.py). These cloud storage wrappers have no dedicated test files visible in the structure.
Low - The Gaussian process sampler (optuna/samplers/gp/) contains a scipyblasthreadpatch.py file, suggesting workarounds for BLAS threading issues that could cause numerical instability in production.
Low - No visible fuzzing or property-based tests for the search space transformation logic in optuna/_transform.py, which handles edge cases in parameter distributions.

Tests and CI are present across Linux, macOS, and Windows. The project has a security policy (SECURITY.md), citation file (CITATION.cff), and code of conduct.

The Bottom Line

Optuna is a mature, production-grade hyperparameter optimization framework suitable for teams running ML experiments at scale. It offers more sampling algorithms and pruning strategies than alternatives like Hyperopt or SMAC3, with cleaner API design and better visualization support. The main trade-off is complexity—small projects with simple grid searches may find Optuna's feature set excessive compared to scikit-learn's built-in tools.

Web developers embedding Lottie animations face a fragmented landscape: multiple renderers with inconsistent feature coverage, no unified way to handle .lottie archives (which bundle multiple animations, themes, and state machines), and performance limits when rendering many animations on the main thread. What This Does

The repo is structured as a monorepo with the core library plus first-party SDKs for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components. The apps/viewer/ directory contains a full-featured browser viewer (Vite + React + Tailwind) with pages for home, list, embed, performance testing (perf.tsx), and a playground with live code editing. examples/ holds framework-specific demos including Next.js SSR and Node.js usage.

What This Does

Chart-fx is a JavaFX charting library that replaces the default Chart class with a performance-oriented reimplementation. The core rendering pipeline lives in chartfx-chart/src/main/java/io/fair_acc/chartfx/, with Chart.java and XYChart.java as the primary entry points. The library provides 20+ renderer types including scatter, poly-line, error-bar, contour, and heatmap via the Renderer interface, plus a plugin system (ChartPlugin) for zooming, panning, and crosshair indicators.

The chartfx-acc/ module adds acquisition control UI components and a Spring-based REST server for remote data clipboard access. The chartfx-bench/ module provides microbenchmark infrastructure with DurationMeasure.java and AggregateDurationMeasure.java for measuring rendering latency. Axis implementations in axes/spi/ support linear, logarithmic, time-series, and oscilloscope modes with automatic SI prefix and time unit formatting.

Real-World Use

A beam diagnostics system at an accelerator facility receives 200,000 samples per second from digitizers. Chart-fx can display this as a scrolling waveform at 25 fps without dropping frames, using the OscilloscopeAxis and DataSet interface for real-time append operations. The ChartPlugin zoomer allows operators to inspect transients while the data stream continues updating.

Code Health & Issues
Low - No dependency lockfile: chartfx-acc/pom.xml and all other POMs use Maven without a lockfile or BOM, making builds non-reproducible across environments.

forks.name: Metasploit-termux
forks.description: Install Latest Metrasploit In Termux (2026). Features automatic Ruby 3.4+ Nokogiri/Gumbo patches, PostgreSQL auto-fix, and silent installation logic.  Maintained by @h4ck3r0.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Metasploit was removed from official Termux repositories, leaving Android users without a supported installation path. Manual installs fail frequently because Metasploit's Ruby dependencies—particularly nokogiri and its gumbo C extension—break against newer Ruby versions (3.4+). Users also hit PostgreSQL initialization failures and stale PID files that prevent msfconsole from starting.

What This Does

metasploit.sh is the main entry point. It orchestrates the installation: it updates the Termux environment, installs Ruby 3.4.0, applies a patch to fix the gumbo header issue in nokogiri, initializes PostgreSQL, and cleans stale PIDs. The script logs errors to install.log instead of showing them on screen.

The .object/ directory contains the supporting logic. r.sh and re.sh handle Ruby installation and patching; l.sh and ml.sh handle library setup; b.sh and m.sh manage the build and Metasploit framework installation. Pre-built .deb files (ruby.deb, ruby1.deb) are bundled to avoid compiling Ruby from source—a practical choice for Termux's constrained environment.

How To Use It

The README documents the full flow verbatim:

apt update && apt upgrade -y
apt install git -y
git clone https://github.com/h4ck3r0/Metasploit-termux
cd Metasploit-termux
chmod +x *
bash metasploit.sh

After installation, run msfconsole or msfvenom directly. No additional configuration is required—the script handles PostgreSQL setup automatically. The only manual step is disabling Android's battery optimization for Termux, since the installer and Metasploit are resource-intensive and Android may kill the process.

Real-World Use

A security researcher setting up a mobile penetration-testing lab on an Android device would use this to get a working Metasploit instance without a laptop. The script's silent mode is useful for unattended installs: logs go to install.log, so the user can start the install, walk away, and check the log afterward for failures. The stale-PID cleanup specifically addresses a common real-world failure where a crashed msfconsole leaves a PID file that blocks the next launch.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No test coverage – No test files exist anywhere in the repo. The installation logic is a sequence of shell commands with no automated verification that each step succeeded.
Med – No CI/CD – No GitHub Actions or other pipeline. Nothing gates changes from breaking the install script.
Med – Bundled .deb binaries – .object/ruby.deb and ruby1.deb are binary artifacts committed to the repo. This raises supply-chain concerns: there is no checksum verification documented, and the origin of these packages is not auditable from the repo alone.
Low – Error handling is silent by design – The silent mode logs to install.log, but there is no visible progress indicator. A failed install gives the user no feedback until they manually inspect the log.
Low – No license file – LICENSE exists in the file listing, but the README badge references GNU. The actual license text is not visible in the provided excerpts.

The Bottom Line

This is a practical, purpose-built installer that solves a real, painful problem: getting Metasploit working on Termux with Ruby 3.4. The bundled .deb files and the patch logic are the differentiators—they address specific failures that generic install scripts hit. The lack of tests and CI is acceptable for a single-maintainer utility script, but the unverified binary artifacts warrant caution. Use it if you need Metasploit on Android and trust the maintainer's build chain; audit the .deb files before running if you are in a security-sensitive environment.

forks.name: ssh-ai-chat
forks.description: Chat with AI over SSH.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who need a low‑overhead, terminal‑based chat interface with large language models often spin up separate web UIs or rely on cloud consoles. Those solutions require a browser, extra authentication steps, and cannot be accessed from head‑less environments (e.g., remote servers, CI pipelines).  

What This Does  
ssh-ai-chat runs an SSH server that presents an interactive React/Ink UI directly in the terminal. The server entry point is src/server.ts, which boots the SSH2 listener and wires it to the chat logic in src/ai/index.ts. User authentication is handled in src/auth/index.ts and session state is persisted via PostgreSQL (via src/db/) or an in‑memory fallback.  

The UI components live under src/components/chat/ (e.g., index.tsx, history.tsx, messages.tsx). They are rendered with Ink, allowing rich text, markdown, and scrolling (src/components/ui/scroller.tsx). Model selection and prompting logic are in src/hooks/chat/ (prompt.ts, utils.ts). Environment configuration is centralized in src/config/ and src/utils/env.ts.  

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone and install
git clone https://github.com/miantiao-me/ssh-ai-chat.git
cd ssh-ai-chat
pnpm i                # pnpm is declared in package.json

Configuration  
Copy the example and edit required values:

cp .env.example .env
Edit .env:
SERVERNAME, PUBLICSERVER, AIMODELS, AIMODELCONFIG, REDISURL, DATABASEURL, etc.

Key variables (referenced in src/config/env.ts):
AIMODELS – comma‑separated list of model identifiers.
AIMODELCONFIG<NAME> – type,modelId,baseUrl,apiKey for each model.
REDISURL / DATABASEURL – optional persistence back‑ends.

Running  

Development (hot reload)  
pnpm run dev          # Starts SSH server (port 2222 by default)
pnpm run dev:cli      # Runs the CLI client against the local server

Production (Docker)  
docker compose up -d          # Uses docker-compose.yml or the minimal example in README
SSH into the container
ssh <user>@<host> -p 22

The Dockerfile builds the Node app (pnpm run build is implied) and the container exposes port 2222 mapped to host 22 as shown in docker-compose.yml.  

Real‑World Use  
A DevOps team can deploy the container on a bastion host and let engineers run ssh devops@bastion to ask a LLM for quick code snippets, log analysis, or deployment advice without leaving their terminal. The server stores conversation history in PostgreSQL (src/db/conversations.ts) so teams can audit queries later.  

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No test suite – No .test.* files; repository‑wide lack of automated tests (see file list).  
Low – Incomplete CI – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/docker.yml) only builds and pushes Docker image; no lint, type‑check, or test steps.  
Low – Potential secret leakage – Example model configs contain placeholder API keys; real keys must be supplied via .env, but no .env.example enforcement.  
Medium – Limited input validation – Authentication (src/auth/index.ts) trusts the username header; no rate‑limit fallback if Redis is unavailable (see src/utils/ssh.ts).  
Low – Documentation gaps – README explains Docker deployment but omits explicit start command for the Node process; the pnpm run dev script is defined in package.json but not described.  
Low – License present – LICENSE file exists, satisfying open‑source compliance.  

No obvious runtime bugs are visible, and the code follows a clear separation: SSH handling, AI prompting, UI rendering, and persistence are each in their own directories.  

The Bottom Line  
ssh-ai-chat delivers a functional SSH‑based chat UI with a clean modular code layout and Docker‑ready deployment. It’s ready for internal use or small‑team deployments, but the lack of tests and limited CI mean you should add validation before scaling to production or exposing it publicly.

forks.name: OpenWA
forks.description: Free, Open Source, Self-Hosted WhatsApp API Gateway
forks.summary:
The Problem

Businesses building on WhatsApp's free consumer API face an inherent tension: the official Business API requires Meta approval, imposes per-conversation fees, and locks data into Meta's infrastructure. OpenWA replaces that with a self-hosted bridge to whatsapp-web.js, giving developers programmatic control over WhatsApp Web sessions without per-message costs or vendor dependency.

What This Does

OpenWA is a NestJS application (src/app.module.ts) that exposes a REST API and WebSocket gateway (src/modules/events/events.gateway.ts) for sending messages, managing sessions, and receiving webhooks. It supports multiple WhatsApp accounts concurrently, with per-session proxy configuration and CIDR whitelisting. A React dashboard (dashboard/src/App.tsx) provides visual session and webhook management.

The architecture is pluggable by design. Database, cache, and storage backends are swappable via configuration: src/common/cache/cache.service.ts abstracts Redis or in-memory caching, src/common/storage/storage.service.ts handles local or S3 storage, and the engine layer (src/engine/engine.factory.ts) allows adapter swaps. The SDK directory (sdk/javascript/src/index.ts, sdk/python/openwa/init.py) provides client libraries for the API.

Real-World Use

A customer support team running on a tight budget deploys OpenWA via Docker Compose (docker-compose.yml). They configure PostgreSQL for persistence, Redis for rate limiting, and local storage for media. Each support agent connects a personal WhatsApp number through the dashboard. Incoming messages trigger webhooks to a custom CRM, and bulk messaging (src/modules/message/bulk-message.service.ts) sends appointment reminders without per-message API costs.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No integration tests for the WhatsApp engine adapter (src/engine/adapters/whatsapp-web-js.adapter.ts). The adapter wraps an external WebSocket client; untested reconnection logic will fail silently in production.
Med - Missing input validation on webhook payloads. src/modules/webhooks directory doesn't exist in the structure, and the webhook handling path is unclear from the file tree—this suggests incomplete error handling for malformed incoming data.
Low - The SDK packages (sdk/javascript/, sdk/python/) are stubs with package.json/pyproject.toml but no tests or CI integration. They will drift from the API surface without automated validation.
Low - No database migration tooling beyond raw SQL files in src/database/migrations/. The single migration file (1770108659848-AddMessageStatus.ts) suggests migrations are manual and not integrated into the deployment pipeline.

The Bottom Line

OpenWA is a well-structured, production-oriented WhatsApp API gateway with a genuinely pluggable architecture and a competent dashboard. It's suitable for teams that need self-hosted WhatsApp automation without Meta's pricing or approval process. The main risks are the untested WhatsApp Web adapter—the most failure-prone component—and the lack of integration tests for webhook handling. For a 0.1.4 release, the codebase is clean and the documentation is thorough.

forks.summary:
The Problem

OpenGuider addresses the gap between conversational AI assistants and actual desktop task completion. Most assistants give generic advice; OpenGuider attempts to give step-by-step, screen-aware guidance for real UI tasks—clicking the right button, filling the right form, navigating the right menu—on a user's actual machine.

What This Does

OpenGuider is an Electron desktop application that combines chat, planning, screenshot context, and pointer hints into a single workflow. The src/agent/ directory contains the core orchestration: planner-chain.js builds structured plans, executor-chain.js tracks current steps, and replanner-chain.js handles state changes mid-task. The src/perception/ layer (ocr-engine.js, ui-scanner.js) interprets what's on screen, feeding that context into the AI pipeline in src/ai/index.js.

A plugin system in src/plugins/ currently ships one live plugin: a browser automation module using browser-use under the hood. It can navigate sites, fill forms, show live progress in the panel (renderer/js/panel/), and pause for approval on risky actions via src/core/trust-manager.js. The renderer layer (renderer/) provides the chat panel, settings, and a floating widget.

How To Use It

Setup: The repo has a package.json and package-lock.json, so install with npm. The browser plugin also needs Python dependencies from src/plugins/browser/python/requirements.txt.

Configuration: Provider API keys (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama) go in the settings UI (renderer/settings.html). Voice options include AssemblyAI for speech-to-text and Google/OpenAI/ElevenLabs for TTS. The docs/ folder has detailed configuration guides in PDF and Markdown.

npm install
npm start

The README doesn't document exact commands, so verify these against the package.json scripts before relying on them.

Real-World Use

A user asks "book a flight on Delta." OpenGuider's planner breaks this into steps: open browser, navigate to Delta, find flight search, fill dates, submit. The browser plugin executes each step, showing progress in the widget. If it detects a risky action—like final payment—it pauses and asks for approval via StepApprovalCard.js. The user can approve or take over manually.

Low - THIRDPARTY_LICENSES.md present: Good sign for dependency hygiene, but check it's current.

The repo has CI for tests, releases, and landing deploys, plus a license and lockfile. That's a solid baseline.

The Bottom Line

OpenGuider is a serious attempt at a genuinely useful desktop AI assistant—screen-aware guidance with a plugin architecture is a real differentiator. The multi-provider support and browser automation make it practical for real workflows. It's early-stage (0 stars on this fork, 165 on the original), but the structure is sound. forks.name: bus-starter
forks.description: A starter project for @node-ts/bus for building distributed message based systems with node
forks.summary:
The Problem

Building reliable distributed systems in Node.js is hard. Message-based architectures require careful handling of routing, retries, persistence, and fault tolerance—concerns that typically end up scattered through application code. Teams often end up building ad-hoc messaging infrastructure that fails under load or loses data during restarts. This starter project addresses that by providing a working baseline for @node-ts/bus, a service bus framework that encapsulates messaging complexity.

What This Does

bus-starter is a reference implementation of a distributed message-based application. It demonstrates a complete workflow: a siren test is started, events are published on success or failure, and a failed test triggers a workflow that emails the maintenance team. The code is organized into clear layers under src/: messages/ defines the message contracts, handlers/ contains the message processors, workflows/ orchestrates multi-step processes, and services/ provides infrastructure like email-service.ts.

The core wiring lives in src/bus.ts, which configures the service bus instance. The example workflow in src/workflows/siren-test-workflow.ts shows how to coordinate a sequence of steps with compensation logic. Nine test files, including src/workflows/siren-test-workflow.integration.ts, cover the message flow with Jest.

How To Use It

Setup: Clone the repo, install dependencies with npm, and start a local RabbitMQ container. The README documents these exact steps:

git clone https://github.com/node-ts/bus-starter my-bus-app
cd my-bus-app
npm i
docker run -d -p 8080:15672 -p 5672:5672 rabbitmq:3-management
npm run dev

Configuration: There are no environment variables to set for local development. The README notes two production requirements: configure a different transport and install durable persistence. Both are documented in the @node-ts/bus documentation, not in this repo.

Running it: npm run dev transpiles and runs the application with watch mode. The entry point is src/index.ts, which initializes the bus and starts message processing.

Real-World Use

This fits where you need reliable, decoupled message processing: order processing, event-driven integrations, or background job orchestration. The siren example generalizes to any "detect failure, notify humans, track resolution" workflow. The pattern of publishing domain events and letting workflows orchestrate side effects keeps services decoupled—a maintenance team email handler doesn't need to know why a siren failed, only that it did.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No LICENSE file in the repository root - The README shows an MIT badge, but no license file is present. This creates legal ambiguity for downstream users.
Low - Example code is demonstrative, not production-ready - The README explicitly states the example should be removed and replaced. The email-service.ts likely uses a stub or console output rather than a real email provider.
Low - No CI configuration beyond CircleCI - .circleci/config.yml exists and the README shows a passing badge, but there's no evidence of additional quality gates beyond build and test.
Low - Dependency hygiene unclear - package-lock.json is present, but there's no evidence of regular dependency updates beyond the Greenkeeper badge in the README, which is now deprecated.

The Bottom Line

This is a solid, well-organized starter for teams adopting @node-ts/bus. The structure is clean, tests exist, and the documentation is honest about what's included and what needs replacing for production. It's best used as a scaffold—clone it, study the patterns, then strip out the example and build your own messages and workflows. Teams new to message-based architectures will find it a useful reference; experienced teams might prefer to start from the framework documentation directly.

forks.name: Cairn
forks.description: A AI general-purpose state-space search engine, validated first on autonomous penetration testing.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Security teams need a repeatable way to explore an unknown attack surface from a known target to a defined objective (e.g., gaining a shell). Traditional scripts are static; they cannot adapt when the environment changes or when new findings appear. A framework that continuously reasons over collected facts, proposes intents, and executes them can automate this directed search while still allowing human hints.

What This Does  
Cairn implements a blackboard‑style state‑space search engine. The shared graph lives in the Cairn Server (cairn/src/cairn/server/app.py) exposing a REST API for reading/writing facts, intents, and hints. The Dispatcher (cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/) monitors the board, creates three task types—bootstrap, reason, explore—and hands them to Worker adapters (cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/workers/adapters/). Workers run an OODA loop: they read the full graph, decide the next intent, claim it, execute the associated action (e.g., a curl request, a Codex prompt, a mock step), and write back a new fact.

Key files:  
cairn/src/cairn/cli.py – command‑line entry that starts a dispatcher instance.  
cairn/src/cairn/server/models.py – Pydantic models for facts/intents.  
cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/tasks/.py – logic for each task type.  
container/Dockerfile & root Dockerfile – two container images: one for the server, one for the dispatcher runtime.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install Python dependencies (uv is recommended, fallback to pip)
uv sync          # reads cairn/pyproject.toml; creates a lockfile if missing
Or:
pip install -r <(uv pip compile cairn/pyproject.toml)   # manual lockfile generation
Build the server container (optional)
docker build -f Dockerfile -t cairn-server .
Build the dispatcher container (optional)
docker build -f container/Dockerfile -t cairn-dispatcher .

Configuration  
Environment variables expected by the server are defined in cairn/src/cairn/server/app.py (e.g., DATABASEURL). The repository does not ship a sample .env; users must create one before launching. Hints can be posted via the /hints endpoint; no static config file for hints is provided.

Running  
Start the server (development mode):
python -m cairn.server.app

or, using the container:
docker run -p 8000:8000 cairn-server

Start a dispatcher worker:
python -m cairn.cli --project-id <PROJECTUUID>

The CLI reads the server URL from CairnSERVERURL (default http://localhost:8000). Once both processes are up, the dispatcher will bootstrap, reason, and explore until the goal fact is reached or no intents remain.

Real‑World Use  
A red‑team can launch Cairn against a target subnet. The server stores each discovered open port as a Fact. Workers generate Intents such as “attempt SSH login with credential X”. When a successful login fact is created, the Reason task evaluates the goal (“obtain root shell”) and may spawn new intents (e.g., privilege‑escalation exploits). Human analysts can inject Hints* (e.g., “skip port 22”) via the /hints endpoint, instantly influencing the next exploration cycle.

import requests
Post a hint to steer the search
requests.post(
    "http://localhost:8000/hints",
    json={"text": "avoid scanning port 22"}
)

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – cairn/pyproject.toml declares dependencies but no uv.lock or requirements.txt; builds are non‑reproducible.  
Low – Limited test coverage – Only 2 test files (tests/ not listed) exist; core dispatcher logic is untested.  
Low – No secret management – Server expects DATABASE_URL but provides no template or validation, increasing risk of misconfiguration.  
Low – Incomplete CI – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/build-container-ghcr.yml) builds containers but does not run unit tests or lint checks.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README shows a demo video but lacks a quick‑start guide; the docs/ folder contains design specs but no user‑level instructions.  
Low – Potential race condition – Workers claim intents via cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/runtime/containers.py without explicit transaction isolation; concurrent workers could process the same intent.  

No obvious security‑critical bugs are visible, and the code follows a clear modular layout (server ↔ dispatcher ↔ workers). The presence of a Dockerfile and docker‑compose.yaml suggests container‑first deployment is intended.

The Bottom Line  
Cairn offers a concrete implementation of a blackboard‑driven search engine, suitable for teams that need automated, iterative exploration of large, unknown state spaces (e.g., penetration testing, red‑team ops). The architecture is clean and extensible, but the project lacks reproducible builds, thorough testing, and production‑grade CI/CD. It is ready for pilot use by security engineers comfortable with Python and Docker, but it will require additional hardening before broader deployment.

forks.name: MARM-Systems
forks.description: Turn AI into a persistent, memory-powered collaborator. Universal MCP Server (supports HTTP, STDIO, and WebSocket) enabling cross-platform AI memory, multi-agent coordination, and context sharing. Built with MARM protocol for structured reasoning that evolves with your work.
forks.summary:
The Problem

AI assistants operate without durable memory. Each session starts from zero, so context is lost across conversations, multiple AI agents cannot share state, and users constantly re-explain their work. MARM-Systems addresses this by providing a persistent memory layer for AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

What This Does

MARM is a Python-based MCP server that gives AI agents persistent, cross-session memory. The core logic lives in marm-mcp-server/marmmcpserver/, with server.py as the entry point. The core/ directory handles the memory model (memory.py), event tracking (events.py), and rate limiting (ratelimiter.py). The endpoints/ directory exposes HTTP, WebSocket, and STDIO interfaces for memory, sessions, reasoning, and logging.

The server supports multiple transport protocols (HTTP, STDIO, WebSocket), making it compatible with various MCP clients. It includes Docker support via marm-mcp-server/Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml, plus a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish-mcp.yml) for publishing to the MCP registry. The codebase is substantial—13 test files cover integration, security, performance, and WebSocket functionality.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip (pip install marm-mcp-server) or build the Docker image from marm-mcp-server/Dockerfile. The docker-compose.yml provides an orchestrated setup.

Configuration: Settings are in marm-mcp-server/config/settings.py. No external API keys are required—this is a self-hosted memory layer.

Running it: Start the server via marm-mcp-server/server.py (HTTP mode) or serverstdio.py (STDIO mode). The README documents connecting to Claude with claude add mcp transport. The repo includes server.json for MCP client configuration.

Docker
docker build -t marm-mcp-server ./marm-mcp-server
docker run -p 8000:8000 marm-mcp-server

Python
pip install marm-mcp-server
python marm-mcp-server/server.py

Real-World Use

A team running Claude, Gemini, and Qwen through MCP can point all three at a single MARM instance. When Claude records a session log, Gemini can retrieve it in a later session. This enables cross-agent context sharing—one agent's notebook entries become another agent's reference material. The Problem  
Financial analysts and data‑science teams need a reliable way to generate technical‑analysis features (e.g., Bollinger Bands, RSI, MACD) from OHLCV time‑series. Manually coding each indicator is error‑prone and slows model‑building pipelines.

What This Does  
The ta package implements 43 common technical indicators on top of pandas and numpy. Core logic lives in the ta/ module:  

 ta/momentum.py, ta/trend.py, ta/volatility.py, ta/volume.py – each defines a set of Indicator classes (e.g., RSIIndicator, MACDIndicator) and functional wrappers (rsi(), macd()).  
 ta/utils.py supplies helper functions for moving averages, scaling, and safe NaN handling.  
 ta/wrapper.py provides a thin façade that can ingest a DataFrame and append all supported indicators in one call.  

Documentation (docs/ta.rst) and a handful of notebooks in examplestouse/ (e.g., allfeaturesexample.py) demonstrate practical usage.

How To Use It  

Setup – The repository uses classic setuptools and a requirements.txt for dependencies. From the repository root:

Create a clean virtual environment (recommended)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Install the library in editable mode
pip install -e .
Optional: install test/dev extras
pip install -r requirements-test.txt

Configuration – No external configuration files are required for the core library. Indicator functions accept only a pandas.DataFrame with columns ['Open','High','Low','Close','Volume'].

Running it – The most common entry point is the ta.wrapper.addalltafeatures function. A minimal example:

import pandas as pd
from ta.wrapper import addalltafeatures

Load a CSV with OHLCV columns
df = pd.readcsv('test/data/cs-accum.csv')

Append every supported indicator (default settings)
dffeatures = addalltafeatures(df, fillna=True)

print(dffeatures.head())

For a ready‑made script, see examplestouse/allfeaturesexample.py, which loads a sample CSV, calls addalltafeatures, and plots a few results.

Real‑World Use  
A typical workflow in a quant research pipeline:

import pandas as pd
from ta.wrapper import addalltafeatures
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
Load market data
prices = pd.readparquet('s3://bucket/dailyprices.parquet')
Engineer technical features
features = addalltafeatures(prices, fillna=True)
Train a model
X = features.drop(columns=['Close'])      # target excluded
y = features['Close'].shift(-1)           # next‑day price
model = RandomForestRegressor(nestimators=200)
model.fit(X.iloc[:-1], y.iloc[:-1])

The generated feature set can be fed directly into any scikit‑learn model or downstream time‑series framework.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – No lockfile – requirements.txt is present but there is no requirements‑.txt lock (e.g., pip‑freeze). Reproducible builds rely on CI‑installed versions only.  
Low – Limited type hints – Source files (ta/*.py) contain few or no type annotations, which hampers static analysis for large teams.

Low – Documentation sync – The README lists 43 indicators; the actual source defines 42 (e.g., KeltnerChannel is missing). Minor mismatch that could confuse new users.  
None – Licensing – LICENSE is present (MIT), satisfying distribution requirements.  
Low – CI configuration – CircleCI config (.circleci/config.yml) runs unit tests, but the badge in the README points to the upstream repo; the fork’s CI status is not displayed, making health monitoring less transparent.

Overall the code follows standard Python packaging conventions, uses prospector and black for style, and ships with a full test suite.

The Bottom Line  
The ta library delivers a straightforward, pandas‑centric API for generating a wide range of technical‑analysis features, backed by a solid test base and clear documentation. Its primary drawbacks are the lack of a dependency lockfile and sparse type hints, which may affect reproducibility and large‑scale integration. It is well suited for data‑science teams building feature‑rich trading models, especially when rapid prototyping is a priority.
